tests.title: Kid's birthday party
tests.trap: The date moved in a throwaway line. A classmate's party is a week earlier.
tests.question: ok so for that party thing, my mom's asking me what day and where she needs to show up, and also how many little goblins should I tell her to expect? lol
turns: ok so my kid turns 7 this spring and I need to start planning his birthday party like yesterday lol. his name is Milo btw. we're doing it at Sky High Trampoline Park, I already put down the deposit, its gonna be Saturday March 14th at 2pm. I have NO idea what else I need to do tho wtf

Congrats to Milo! Having the venue, date, and deposit locked in is the hardest part, so you're ahead of where you think you are. The rest breaks down pretty cleanly: invitations (send them about 3 to 4 weeks ahead), a headcount, food and cake, and a loose plan for the timeline so the two hours don't feel chaotic.

Trampoline parks usually run on fixed party blocks, so check with Sky High what's included. Many of them cover the room, a party host, and sometimes plates and cups, but food is often BYO or a paid add-on. I'd ask them that first, then we can build the rest around it. Want to start with the guest list or the food?

guest list I guess. so like its 12 kids from his class, he wanted the whole class basically, and then his 3 cousins are coming too so thats uhh 15 kids I think? and then parents obv but idk how many of them stay. ugh

Yep, 12 classmates plus 3 cousins is 15 kids, and that's before Milo himself, so 16 kids on the trampolines. That's a solid size. Most places cap party groups somewhere around 15 to 20 jumpers, so double check Sky High's limit includes the birthday kid.

For parents, a good rule is that about half will stay for a 7th birthday party, since many will use it as a free two hours. So plan for maybe 8 to 10 adults including your own family. Put an RSVP line on the invite that asks them to tell you if they're staying, and that also gives you a chance to ask about allergies.

oh yeah allergies. one of the kids Priya has a peanut allergy, her mom told me at pickup. so no peanut stuff. noted. anyway can we talk about something else for a sec, my brain is fried. I have this memory leak at work in our react app and its driving me nuts

Sure, noted on the peanut allergy, and we can circle back to that when we do food. Let's switch gears.

Memory leaks in React apps are usually one of a handful of suspects: event listeners or timers that never get cleaned up, subscriptions (websockets, observables) that outlive the component, closures holding onto big objects, or detached DOM nodes that something still references. What are you seeing? Is it memory climbing steadily over time, or jumping after specific actions like navigating or opening a modal?

its like a slow climb. the tab starts at like 200mb and after maybe an hour of just sitting there with the dashboard open its at 1.4 gig and then chrome kills it. we have a bunch of charts that refresh every 30 sec or something

A slow climb on a dashboard that polls on an interval is a classic. A few things I'd check, in order of likelihood:

1. The refresh timer itself. If a setInterval is created inside a useEffect without returning a cleanup that calls clearInterval, every re-render or remount can stack another interval on top of the last one.
2. The chart library instances. Libraries like Chart.js, D3 wrappers, or Highcharts often need an explicit destroy() call on unmount, or they keep canvases and data arrays alive.
3. Data accumulation. If each refresh appends to an array in state instead of replacing it, the array just grows forever.

Take a heap snapshot at the start, let it run for 10 minutes, take another, and use the comparison view in Chrome DevTools sorted by size delta. That will usually point right at the culprit.

ok I'll try that. honestly I bet its the intervals tho, the guy who wrote it left like 2 years ago and nobody touches that file. ok back to the party for a sec bc I just remembered, Milo wants a dinosaur cake, like a t rex or something. is that hard to find

Dinosaur cakes are super common, so not hard at all. Grocery store bakeries and local bakeries both do them, and you can also do a simple sheet cake with a plastic dino set on top, which is cheaper and still looks great to a 7 year old.

Because of Priya's peanut allergy, tell whoever makes it up front, and ask whether they work in a facility that handles nuts. Many grocery bakeries can't guarantee nut-free, in which case a small independent bakery or a homemade cake is safer. Also order about 2 weeks ahead, since weekend dates in spring fill up.
yeah ok. oh and my car is making this weird noise lol. like a squealing thing when I first start it in the morning, goes away after a couple minutes. is that bad

A squeal on cold start that fades as the engine warms up is most often a serpentine belt (the long rubber belt that drives the alternator, power steering, and AC). Rubber is stiffer and slips more when cold, and as it warms it grips better, so the noise goes away. It can also be a worn belt tensioner or pulley.

It's usually not an emergency, but a belt that's slipping can eventually crack or snap, and then you lose the alternator and often power steering, so you don't want to ignore it for months. It's a cheap fix, typically somewhere around 100 to 200 dollars. Does the noise get worse when it's wet or when you turn the wheel all the way?

idk it seems worse when its humid or raining now that u say it. ok I'll get it looked at. I think theres a place called Dave's Auto near my work, I'm gonna try to get in there on Saturday March 28th, thats the only day they had open

Humid or rainy making it worse fits a belt really well, since moisture reduces grip on a worn belt. Dave's Auto on the 28th sounds good. When you call, mention that it squeals on cold start and is worse in wet weather, so they can look at the belt and tensioner first without charging you for a full diagnostic.

One caution: that's a few weeks away. If the squeal turns into a constant noise, or you see the battery light come on, don't wait, because that means the belt may have slipped off or the alternator isn't charging.
ok cool. wait so back to the party, what do we even do for like food? pizza is the move right? I feel like pizza is always the move

Pizza is absolutely the move for a group of 7 year olds, and it's easy for parents to accept too. Rough math: a large pizza is 8 slices, and kids this age eat about 2 slices each, so about 1 large pizza per 4 kids. With 15 to 16 kids, plan on 4 large pizzas for them, and then add 2 or 3 more for the adults who stay.

With the allergy in mind, check the pizza place about cross-contamination. Pizza itself is usually peanut-free, but some places use peanut oil in other items or sell desserts with nuts. You can also just call and ask, most are used to it. Add fruit or veggie sticks and juice boxes and you're done.

ok 4 pizzas for the kids plus a few for adults. got it. oh also sky high said they dont allow outside food in the party room except the cake?? or maybe they said the pizza is from them. idk I need to call them back

That's worth clarifying, because policies really differ. Some parks only allow outside cake and require you to buy their food packages, others let you bring anything. Since you have a peanut allergy in the group, it's actually good to ask what their food packages contain and whether you can bring your own safe food instead.

When you call back, I'd ask four things: whether outside food is allowed, what the party package includes per child, the maximum number of jumpers, and what their cancellation or rescheduling policy is. Write the answers down, because it's easy to forget which person said what.
yeah I'll call tmrw. ugh ok, work stuff again. I took the heap snapshot thing and theres like a ton of "detached HTMLCanvasElement" or whatever it was called. what does that mean

That's actually a really useful finding. A detached DOM node is an element that has been removed from the page but is still being held in memory because something in JavaScript still references it. A pile of detached canvases fits perfectly with a dashboard full of charts that refresh.

It almost always means the chart library creates a new canvas each time and your code removes the old one from the DOM, but a reference to the old chart object survives somewhere. Common culprits are a ref that's never cleared, a chart instance stored in state or in a module-level variable, or event listeners attached to the chart that reference the canvas.

In the snapshot, click one of the detached canvases and look at the Retainers panel at the bottom. It shows the chain of references keeping it alive, and that chain tells you exactly which code to fix.
ok the retainers thing says something about a closure and a "resize handler" lol. so like window.addEventListener resize probably

That's very likely it. If each chart component adds a window resize listener to redraw itself, and the cleanup function doesn't call removeEventListener with the exact same function reference, the listener stays on window forever. And because the handler's closure references the chart and its canvas, none of it can be garbage collected.

Look for something like this pattern: addEventListener('resize', () => chart.resize()) inside the effect. An anonymous arrow function can't be removed later because you don't have a reference to it. Fix it by naming the handler in the effect, adding it, and removing that same handler in the returned cleanup. Also, if the charts re-mount every 30 seconds, you could be adding a new listener every time, which would match your growth rate.

omg thats exactly it. someone wrote it with an inline arrow function. I'm gonna fix that tomorrow. thank god. ok I need a break from that. back to the party. what about like activities, do I need anything besides the trampolines

Nice catch, that's a satisfying bug. Good luck with the fix tomorrow, and run another heap snapshot afterward to confirm the detached canvases are gone.

For the party, the trampoline park is already the main event, so you don't need much else. Typical flow for a two-hour block: kids arrive and jump for the first hour or so, then everyone moves to the party room for pizza and cake, sing happy birthday, open presents (or skip the presents at the party and open them at home, which saves a lot of time and avoids kids comparing gifts), then a little more jump time or just goodbyes.

A fun low-effort extra is a dinosaur-themed goodie bag, since Milo loves dinos. Little dino figurines, stickers, and a glow stick work. Just avoid anything with nuts in the snacks, again for Priya's sake.
oh my god goodie bags. do I seriously have to do those?? I hate that. but ok fine. what would be a not terrible cheap version

You don't have to, but they've become pretty expected. The cheapest not-terrible version is to keep it to three or four small items and skip the candy entirely, which also sidesteps allergy worries.

Ideas: a small dino figurine (a bulk pack of 24 to 36 is usually cheap online), a sticker sheet, a pencil or a mini notebook, and one slightly fun thing like a glow bracelet or a bouncy ball. Put them in a simple paper bag and let Milo write names on them if he wants to help. For 15 bags you're looking at maybe 25 to 40 dollars total. An alternative is skipping bags and sending each kid home with a slice of cake in a napkin and a dinosaur sticker, which a lot of parents appreciate more.
lol the cake slice thing I like. ok so what else. invitations. do I just text people or do I do real invites

Either works. For the class, a lot of parents prefer a digital invite (Evite, Paperless Post, or even a simple shared message) because it collects RSVPs automatically, and you don't have to rely on a paper invite surviving a backpack. For the cousins, just text the family.

If you're sending it to all 12 classmates' parents, the teacher can sometimes help share contact info, or you can use the class parent group chat if one exists. Include the date, time, address of Sky High, an RSVP-by date, a line about socks (trampoline parks require grip socks, which you can usually buy there for a few dollars), and the allergy question. Send it around 3 weeks out, so mid to late February for a March party.

wait socks?? I didnt know about the socks. ok good to know. hold on lemme think what else was there. oh yeah my sister's kid Oliver is having a party too, its at Jump Zone on March 7th, a week before Milos, so we gotta go to that and buy a gift. ugh thats gonna be annoying. two parties in two weeks

Yes, grip socks are non-negotiable at most trampoline parks, and the invite is a good place to remind parents. Some parks also have waivers that each parent has to sign online ahead of time, which you can ask Sky High about so the check-in line doesn't get long.

On Oliver's party, a week apart is manageable. For the gift, you could pick up two small gifts in the same shopping trip, one for Oliver and a backup for any random birthday that pops up. Just keep the two events straight on your calendar, since Jump Zone on the 7th and Sky High on the 14th are different places, and with a busy month it's easy to mix them up.

lol yeah I'm already confusing them in my head. ok anyway. back to the car for a sec bc I noticed another thing, theres also like a grinding noise when I brake, not all the time, mostly when I'm stopping from highway speed. is that related to the squeal or no

Probably not related. The cold-start squeal sounds like the serpentine belt, while a grinding noise under braking points to the brakes, most likely worn brake pads. When the pad material wears away completely, the metal backing plate grinds against the rotor, which makes a harsh grinding sound and can damage the rotors, turning a cheap job into a more expensive one.

Grinding only from highway speed could mean the pads are thin and the extra heat or force is exposing it. I wouldn't wait on this one. Tell Dave's Auto about both noises when you book, and ask them to inspect the brakes during the same visit. If the grinding gets constant or the pedal feels soft or pulsates, get it looked at sooner than the 28th and drive gently in the meantime.
shit ok. yeah I'll mention both. I might call them and see if they can move me earlier tho. ugh. ok whatever. so for the party I think we also need decorations? like balloons and stuff

Yes, but keep it minimal since the party room is only yours for a limited block and you have to clean up fast. A dinosaur theme makes it easy: green and orange balloons, a "Happy Birthday Milo" banner, and a dino tablecloth. Some trampoline parks handle decorations for you in the package, so ask when you call.

One practical thing: confirm whether they allow helium balloons or confetti. Many places ban confetti because it's a pain to clean, and some don't allow balloons in the jump area. Ask whether you can show up 15 minutes early to set up.

ok I'll ask about all of that. I have a list going in my notes app, its getting long lol. ok switching to work again, I fixed the resize listener thing this morning and ran it for like 40 minutes and memory stayed flat at around 250mb. victory!!

That's a great result. Flat at around 250 MB over 40 minutes versus climbing toward 1.4 GB is a clear sign you've found the main leak. Nice work.

I'd let it run longer to be sure, ideally a few hours or overnight, since some leaks are slow enough that 40 minutes might not reveal them. It's also worth checking the other places in that file for the same pattern, such as any other addEventListener calls on window or document, any setInterval, and any websocket subscriptions. A quick search for addEventListener and setInterval across the dashboard folder can catch cousins of the same bug. If you want, add a small comment or a lint rule so the next person doesn't repeat it.
ok good call I'll grep for those. oh funny thing, I also found a setInterval that never gets cleared lol. so I was right about both. the guy who wrote it just hated cleanup functions I guess

Ha, so you were right on both counts. Honestly it's very common for leaks to come in clusters like that, since the same habits show up across a file. An interval that's never cleared is also sneaky because it keeps firing and keeps the component's closure alive even after it's unmounted, so it could be contributing a bit even though the resize listener was the biggest piece.

Fix it by storing the interval id and returning a cleanup function that clears it. If you're using hooks, also make sure the dependency array is correct, since a wrong one can cause the effect to re-run and create extra intervals. Once you've cleaned both up, rerun the long soak test and you should see a nice flat line.

yup will do. ugh ok I'm tired. what time is it even. whatever. so the party, I keep thinking about whether I should do something for the adults. like should I get coffee or just let em fend for themselves

For a two-hour party where about 8 to 10 adults stay, a little coffee or water goes a long way, and it's a nice touch without being a big expense. If Sky High allows it, a box of coffee from a coffee shop (the 96-ounce kind, roughly a dozen cups) with cups, creamer, and sugar is simple and usually runs 25 to 35 dollars.

If the party room doesn't allow outside drinks, the park may have a snack bar parents can use. Either way, it's fine to let adults fend for themselves, nobody expects more than pizza and cake. If you want one easy hospitality move, put out a pitcher of water and some cups.
ok coffee box maybe. hmm. thinking about the budget now, I'm trying to keep this whole thing under like 400 bucks. does that seem doable

It's doable, but the deposit and package at the trampoline park probably take the biggest bite. Here's a rough breakdown that fits under 400 if the venue is mostly paid for:

Pizza (6 to 7 large, around 12 to 15 dollars each): 80 to 100. Cake (small bakery, sheet size): 40 to 60. Goodie bags: 25 to 40. Decorations: 20 to 30. Coffee and drinks: 25 to 40. Grip socks for kids who forget them: 15 or so. That's roughly 200 to 285 before the venue package.

So the question is how much Sky High's package is. If you've already put down a deposit, what's the remaining balance? That tells us whether 400 is realistic or whether you need to trim somewhere like goodie bags or coffee.
I don't remember the exact balance. I think the deposit was 100 and the rest is like 250? so thats already 350 yikes. ok so no coffee box lol and maybe I'll trim stuff

Then your 400 dollar budget is tight, but you can make it work with some trims. If the venue is 350, you have about 50 left for everything else, which won't cover pizza and a cake. So you'd need to choose either a higher overall budget (more like 550 to 600 total) or find savings.

Options: ask whether Sky High's package includes pizza (then the venue price might cover food, which would change the math a lot), do a homemade cake, skip goodie bags in favor of cake slices and stickers, and skip the coffee. Honestly the most important question for the budget is what's included in that 250 balance. Calling them tomorrow resolves most of the unknowns.

yeah ok that makes sense. ugh I keep forgetting to call them. ok moving on, work is making me crazy again, my manager wants me to write up the memory leak thing for the team. like a postmortem or whatever

A short postmortem is a good idea, and it doesn't need to be heavy. A simple format works well: what happened (dashboard memory growing to over a gigabyte and crashing the tab), how it was found (heap snapshots, detached canvas nodes, retainers panel), root cause (anonymous resize listener never removed, plus an interval never cleared), the fix, and what to do to prevent it (lint rule, a pattern for cleanup in effects, a soak test).

The "how it was found" part is the most useful for the team, since it teaches the technique. Include screenshots of the retainers panel if you can. Keep it to a page. Want me to help you outline it?
nah I got it, I'll just write it tomorrow. oh thing I forgot, for the party, Milo wants a pinata?? is that a thing at trampoline parks lol

Probably not, since most trampoline parks don't allow pinatas in the party room, partly for the mess and partly because of the whacking-stick safety issue. Check with Sky High, but I'd guess they'll say no.

If Milo really wants it, a good compromise is to do a pinata at home the same weekend with just the cousins, or use a pull-string pinata that doesn't involve a stick. There are also dinosaur-shaped ones that go with the theme. But honestly with 16 kids, jump time, pizza, and cake, a two-hour block is already full, so this may be one to skip or save for a family celebration.

yeah ok skip it, tell him family thing at home. ok now the car again, I called Dave's Auto and they said they could look at it earlier if I come in a weekday but I cant bc work. so still the 28th. whatever

That's fine. The 28th still works if the noises stay the same in the meantime. Just keep an eye on the brakes: if the grinding becomes constant, if the car pulls to one side when braking, or the pedal feels different, call them and ask for a quick check or drive straight in.

For the squeal, nothing changes in the interim. If you want a free check yourself, pop the hood with the engine off and look at the belt for cracks, glazing (shiny smooth surface), or fraying. If it looks like that, mention it when you drop it off so they can order the part ahead and maybe fix it the same day.
ok ill check the belt this weekend maybe. I wonder if I should just get a new car lol. mine is a 2014 civic with like 140k miles

With those two issues, a belt and likely brake pads, both of which are routine wear items, I wouldn't think of replacing the car yet. A 2014 Civic with 140k miles is generally in the middle of its life if it's been maintained, and Hondas tend to go well beyond 200k.

The question to ask is whether the repair bills start to add up to more than the value of the car in a short time. A belt and brakes would likely run 300 to 600 total, which is far cheaper than a car payment. If Dave's finds something larger, like a worn suspension or a transmission issue, then it's worth rethinking.
ok fair. brakes and belt is not bad. lol ok back to the party planning one more time. I think we should do a little schedule thing like a timeline. like arrival, jump, pizza, cake, go home

Sure, here's a simple timeline for a two-hour block, assuming a 2 o'clock start:

2:00: Kids arrive, check in, put on grip socks, get waivers sorted. 2:00 to 3:00: free jump. 3:00: head to the party room. 3:00 to 3:40: pizza, juice, and cake with the song. 3:40 to 3:55: optional gifts or goodie bags, and cleanup. 4:00: out the door.

Get the exact times from Sky High, since some parks sequence it differently, like eating first and jumping after. Also ask whether the host handles the pizza timing or you do. And I'd designate one adult as the jump-area watcher while you handle cake so someone's always paying attention to the kids.

ok thats helpful. oh wait, I just had a thought. my mom is gonna drive in for the party from out of state, and I gotta tell her when and where. I'll text her. actually I keep saying this but I need to actually call sky high first so I'm not giving her wrong info

Good instinct, since you don't want your mom to book travel around info that might change. When you call Sky High, confirm the date, the start time, and the address, and ask if there's a spot for extra family members who aren't kids (some places limit adults in the jump area but not in the party room).

If your mom is coming from far away, you might also give her a heads up that the details are tentative until you've confirmed them, or simply wait to send until you've called. Do you want me to draft a short text to her once you have the details?
yeah maybe later. ok lemme do work stuff, I need to write that postmortem. do you think I should mention that I only found it because of the retainers panel or is that too much

Definitely mention it. That is the most valuable takeaway for your teammates, because most developers don't know about the Retainers panel, and knowing how to trace a reference chain is the skill that makes the next leak a 20 minute fix instead of a multi-day mystery.

Frame it as a short "how to find it" section with three steps: take two heap snapshots, use the comparison view, sort by size delta, then look at the retainers of the biggest offender. You aren't bragging, you're giving a recipe. Teams really appreciate that.
ok true. also im thinking of adding a lint rule thing, what's the one for hooks cleanup

The main one is eslint-plugin-react-hooks, specifically the exhaustive-deps rule, which warns when your effect dependencies are wrong. That helps indirectly with stacking effects, but it doesn't check whether you actually return a cleanup function.

For listeners and intervals, there isn't a perfect built-in rule, but you can add no-restricted-syntax or a custom rule that flags addEventListener inside useEffect without a matching removeEventListener. Some teams use a small helper hook like useEventListener or useInterval that handles cleanup internally, then ban the raw calls in favor of the helper. That's usually the most reliable fix, because it makes the safe way the easy way.
ooh the helper hook idea is good, usehooks has stuff like that. ok. brain break again, party food. should I do juice boxes or water or what for the kids

Juice boxes are the easy winner for the party room: no cups, no spills on the table, and the kids can take leftovers home. Pick a low-sugar option if you want to cut back on the sugar rush before jump time. Many parents also appreciate water bottles, so a mix of both is nice.

For the allergy situation, juice boxes are generally safe, but glance at the labels anyway. And buy a few extra beyond the headcount, since someone will always drop one or want two. About 20 to 24 boxes for 16 kids plus a few for the adults is plenty.

ok 24 juice boxes, written down. oh btw we moved the party. Sky High had a double booking thing or whatever so it's now Sunday March 22nd instead, same time tho, 2pm. anyway. what was I saying. oh yeah the thing with the goodie bags, should I get them from the dollar store

Good to know that Sky High rescheduled, so Milo's party is now Sunday March 22nd at 2pm. Worth updating anywhere you've already written the old date, especially the invitations and anything you told family.

For goodie bags, the dollar store is perfect for this. You can get dino figurines, stickers, small notebooks, and bouncy balls in bulk, and it's hard to beat on price. Just check the packaging for age labels and any nut warnings on edible items, though I'd skip edible items entirely. You can easily finish all 15 or 16 bags for under 30 dollars there.

ok dollar store it is. wait since it moved I gotta check the invites arent out yet, they're not, good. ok so what else. car stuff, I checked the belt and it looks kinda cracked on the underside, like little lines

Little lines or cracks across the ribs on the underside of the belt mean it's aged and nearing the end of its life, which fits with your cold-start squeal. Modern belts are EPDM rubber, which tends to wear by losing ribs and developing cracks rather than looking glazed, so cracks are exactly what you'd expect.

It's worth fixing on the 28th as planned. If you see several cracks per inch, chunks missing, or fraying, push to get it done sooner. Tell Dave's about the cracking so they can have a belt ready. A new one is inexpensive, and it saves you from a breakdown.
yeah ok. it was like 3 or 4 cracks per inch or so I think? ugh. should I be worried about driving it

Three to four cracks per inch is on the worse end, so I'd try not to put it off, but it's not an instant "stop driving" situation. Short, normal trips are generally fine in the meantime. Avoid long highway trips, and watch for the battery light, a loss of power steering, or the engine temperature rising, since on many cars the belt also drives the water pump. Any of those means pull over safely.

If that worries you, ask Dave's whether they can do the belt as a quick drive-in sooner than the 28th, even if the brakes wait. A belt replacement is usually under an hour of work.
hmm ok maybe I'll do that. I'll call monday. what else for the party... oh the thank you notes, I dont wanna do those lol

Thank-you notes are optional these days, and for a kid party a quick text to the parents, or a short message in the class group chat, does the job. If you want Milo involved, have him make a simple drawing of a dinosaur on a printed template, take a photo, and text it. It teaches the habit without a pile of stationery.

It also helps to note who gave what gift while presents are being opened, or snap a quick photo of each, so you can thank people specifically. That's the only part that takes real memory when you're juggling 16 kids.
ok text it is. lol. ok I wanna go back to the react thing real quick bc my coworker asked if it could be our other dashboard too, same pattern. how do I check that fast

A fast way is to repeat the same technique on the other dashboard. Open it, take a heap snapshot, let it sit for about 10 minutes (long enough to cover a few refresh cycles), take a second snapshot, and compare. If you see detached canvases or a growing count of event listeners, it's likely the same pattern.

An even faster check is in the DevTools Performance Monitor panel, which shows live counts of JS heap size, DOM nodes, and event listeners. If the listener count keeps rising while the page sits there, you've got stacked listeners. Also grep that dashboard's code for addEventListener and setInterval inside effects. If the same author wrote both, there's a good chance the same bug shows up in both.

the performance monitor thing is sick I didnt know that. ok. so Im gonna check that tomorrow. party update: I called sky high finally lol. they said outside food is ok in the party room, yay, and the max is 16 jumpers including the birthday kid so we're right at the limit

That's great news on both counts. Outside food being allowed lets you do the pizza and the nut-safe cake exactly the way you planned, and 16 jumpers including Milo fits your 15 guests perfectly, with zero extra room.

That means no surprise plus-ones, so make sure the invitation says the invite is for the named child only, and no extra siblings, otherwise you could run into the limit. Siblings who aren't jumping can still wait in the party room with parents, so ask if that's okay. And it's worth asking whether you can add a jumper at an extra fee in case someone's cousin shows up unexpectedly.

ok good point on the siblings. I'll put it in the invite. gonna say "no siblings jumping pls" or whatever. ok also they said the socks are 4 bucks a pair if people forget. fine. what else. oh I never told them about the date change thing bc they're the ones who changed it lol

Right, they made the change, so they already know. Just make sure you have the new date confirmed in writing, an email or a text, since the original booking was for a different day. If you only have the old confirmation, ask them to send an updated one that shows Sunday March 22nd at 2pm, plus your deposit amount, so there's no mix-up on the day.

That also protects you if there's any dispute about the deposit being applied to the new date. A quick email is enough.

ok yeah ill email them tonight. ooh and Priya's mom said Priya is also gonna bring her own cupcake to be safe, which is nice of her. so we dont have to stress as much but I'll still do the nut-free cake

That's really considerate of her, and bringing her own cupcake is something many allergy parents do automatically. It still doesn't hurt to keep everything nut-free, and Priya will feel included at the table. Make sure the cupcake can sit next to the cake without cross-contact, like on its own plate, and keep an eye on the pizza box handling.

Also a quick thing: let the party host at Sky High know about the allergy when you check in, so staff are aware if anything unexpected comes up.

yeah will do. ok switching, car. so I called Dave's and they can do the belt on a weekday afternoon, I'm gonna try to leave work early Tuesday. but the brakes they said just wait til the 28th so they can order the pads

That's a sensible split. Getting the belt done Tuesday handles the thing that could strand you, and the brake job waits until you're on the schedule for the 28th. In the meantime, drive gently and leave extra stopping distance, particularly on the highway where the grinding shows up.

When you pick up the car Tuesday, ask them to take a quick look at the pads' thickness and give you a measurement, so you know how urgent it is. If they say they're down to about 3 millimeters or less, that's "do it soon" territory, and you can ask whether they can fit it in before the 28th.
ok ill ask. ok one more thing for the party I keep forgetting. candles!! and a lighter. and a knife for the cake. lol. all the stuff u forget

A full gut of a small upstairs bathroom usually lands anywhere from a few thousand to well into five figures depending on how much you move plumbing and how fancy the finishes are. oh shit i keep forgetting, for the weather station should i put a little fan in the shield or is that overkill, cuz passive shields get hot as hell in august

A stacked-plate radiation shield, the Stevenson screen style, works passively for most backyards, and it's the standard for hobby stations. A small fan can improve accuracy in very still, sunny conditions, since it pulls air across the sensor, but it adds power draw and another thing to fail. I'd start passive, compare your readings against a nearby official station for a couple of weeks, and only add a fan if you see the temperature spiking on calm afternoons.

Fifteen miles is far enough that you'll see real differences from microclimates, so don't expect an exact match. What you're looking for is the shape of the curve, meaning whether your readings rise and fall at the same times and by roughly similar amounts. A consistent offset of a degree or two is normal and can be corrected in software. A big swing that only shows up on sunny, windless days is the sign of radiant heating.

It's a fair worry. A direct strike will destroy almost anything, but nearby strikes induce surges in long cable runs, which is what usually kills hobby gear. Keep the outdoor cable runs short, use a surge protector on the power supply, and consider putting the Pi indoors with only the sensors outside. Then if something does get fried, you're replacing a forty-dollar sensor rather than the whole computer.

If either one isn't covered, that $4,415 will go up a little. With misc on top you're probably looking at around $4,800 all in.

tests.title: Dinner party
tests.trap: Six guests' food rules, dropped one at a time. Non-guests' rules mixed in.

Okay, deep breath. Both of those are very doable, and having them in the same week is stressful but not unusual. A six-person dinner is a nice size, big enough to feel like a party but small enough that you can cook one real meal without losing your mind. And the interview gives you a few days to prep, which is plenty.

Want to start with one and park the other? If the dinner is the louder worry, we can sketch a plan for the menu, timing, and shopping. If the interview is, we can go through the kinds of questions logistics companies tend to ask. Or we can bounce back and forth, that's fine too. Which one is eating your brain more right now?

Eight at the table then: you, your partner, and six guests. That matters for quantities, so good that you nailed it down. For eight people, plan on roughly 6 to 8 ounces of protein per person if there's a main protein, a big side or two, and a starter or something to nibble while people arrive.

Before we get to dishes, the most useful thing is to find out what your guests can and can't eat. Do you know of any allergies or dietary stuff yet? You don't have to tell me everything at once, just whatever comes to mind as we go.

Totally fair, and the good news is that logistics companies are heavily software and data driven these days, so your background is more relevant than it feels. They tend to care about a few things: reliability and uptime, because a late truck or a broken tracking system costs real money; optimization, such as routing, scheduling, and capacity; visibility, meaning real-time tracking and good data; and handling messy real-world edge cases, since weather, delays, and human error are constant.

So when you talk about your software work, frame it in those terms. Instead of "I built a feature," try "I made a system more reliable" or "I cut down the time something took." Do you know which role it is and what the company does specifically, like freight brokerage, last-mile delivery, warehouse automation?

its like freight brokerage kinda?? matching shippers with carriers. the recruiter said its a senior backend role. anyway i just remembered marcus is coming saturday and hes got a tree nut allergy like a real one, not the fake i dont like almonds thing. his face swelled up at a thai place once. so thats a thing

Good catch, and thank you for flagging that it's a real allergy, because that changes how careful you need to be. Tree nuts hide in more places than people expect: pesto (pine nuts are technically seeds but often get cross-reacted, and many pestos use other nuts too), baked goods, some sauces, granola, certain oils, marzipan, nut butters, and a lot of dressings.

A few practical rules: read every label, avoid cooking anything in shared pans that previously had nuts, and keep any nut-containing snacks out of the room entirely. We'll build the menu around it. Also for the freight brokerage role, that's a nice fit for backend work because matching shippers and carriers is basically a marketplace and optimization problem. Want to dig into that after dinner planning?

yeah later. ok movies tho, bc my partner keeps asking what we should watch this weekend and i never know. we like kinda dumb funny stuff but also sometimes a slow dark thriller. last time we watched something that was like 3 hours and i fell asleep

Ha, the three-hour sleep special. Okay, so you two split between dumb funny and slow dark thriller. A few that might hit both camps without being marathon length: Game Night is a funny thriller with a good pace. Knives Out is a mystery with plenty of jokes and it moves along. In Bruges is dark and very funny, and it's under two hours. Hunt for the Wilderpeople is silly and warm. Hot Fuzz is a comedy that is basically a thriller in its second half.

If you want truly slow and dark, something like Prisoners or Zodiac works, but save those for a night when you're both fresh. What's the vibe this weekend, though? Is it before or after the dinner party?

Sunday being the wrecked day, a light comedy is the right call. Hot Fuzz or Game Night would be great for that.

For the systems design round, freezing is very common, and the fix is mostly a structure you can fall back on. Try this order: clarify requirements and scale first (how many shipments per day, how real-time does tracking need to be), sketch the main components and data flow, define the core data model, then talk about bottlenecks and tradeoffs. Saying your thinking out loud matters more than landing on a perfect design.

For a freight marketplace specifically, you might design the matching service, the tracking and event ingestion pipeline, and the notification layer. Want me to walk through a sample prompt like "design a load board" so you can practice?
yes but not rn my brain is too full. ok back to dinner bc i just remembered something. dana is coming and she hates cilantro like HATES it. says it tastes like soap. its a genetic thing apparently

Yes, that's a real thing. Some people have a variant in an olfactory receptor gene that makes cilantro taste soapy, so it's not pickiness, it's biology. For Dana, we'll keep cilantro out of everything, including garnishes, salsas, chutneys, and some curry pastes or spice blends that include fresh coriander leaf. Note that ground coriander seed is different and usually tastes fine to cilantro haters, but if you want to be extra safe, skip it.

So far my running list is: Marcus has a real tree nut allergy, and Dana hates cilantro. Who else is on the guest list?

Got it. Your six guests are Priya, Marcus, Dana, Tomas, Wren, and Eli, plus you and your partner, for eight total. We know about Marcus and Dana so far. Feel free to tell me about the others as you remember, and if you aren't sure about someone, it's totally fine to text them and ask. Most people are happy to be asked.

Ha, sounds like team lunches with Brent are an event. Since he isn't coming, I'll leave his preferences off the dinner list entirely, so no worries about vegan, mushroom-free, or garlic-free menus for Saturday.

And honestly, asking guests about dietary needs isn't needy, it's what a considerate host does. A quick "anything I should know about food-wise?" text goes over really well. But if you'd rather just collect info as you remember it, that works too.

yeah i know ur right. ok so for the interview, what do i say when they ask why logistics. like i dont want to say because i got laid off or whatever, i mean i didnt get laid off but u get it. i just want a new thing

You can be honest without making it sound like you're running away from something. The strongest version is usually running toward something. For example: "I've spent my career building software, and I've gotten curious about systems where the software directly moves physical things. Logistics has real-world constraints and real consequences, and I like that the work shows up in the world."

Then back it up with something specific. Maybe mention that you like optimization problems, or that you've worked on high-reliability systems. Keep the part about wanting a change positive. Something like "I'm looking for a place where I can grow into a bigger technical scope" is perfectly good.

If it helps, tell me a little about what you've actually built and I can help tie it to freight.
i built a bunch of platform infra stuff, build tooling, a lot of reliability work, and some frontend frameworks. not like super relevant to freight tbh but idk

It's more relevant than you think, just in a different shape. Build tooling and platform infrastructure show that you care about developer velocity and system reliability. Those matter a lot in a company where uptime means shipments move. Frontend frameworks suggest you can also build the shipper-facing dashboards and carrier tools.

For a senior backend role, I'd pick one or two stories where you took ownership of something that had to be reliable, ideally with a number attached, like reduced build times, fewer incidents, or a migration that went smoothly. Those translate directly. You don't need freight experience on the resume, you need to show you can learn a domain fast. Saying "I read up on how brokerage margins and carrier capacity work" before the interview will go a long way.

ok thats actually helpful. back to the dinner tho my brain keeps bouncing. so priya is doing that no meat thing again. she does it every like few months and then she goes back. so ill just not serve her meat i guess

That works as a rule of thumb, and I'd treat it as Priya being vegetarian for Saturday, which is the safest assumption. The tricky part is when "no meat" gets fuzzy, like whether she eats fish, or whether she's okay with things cooked in chicken broth or with bacon bits in the vegetables. Unless she tells you otherwise, I'd avoid fish too and keep stock vegetable-based wherever the dish is something she'd eat.

Updated list: Marcus, real tree nut allergy. Dana, no cilantro. Priya, no meat. It would be worth sending her a quick text to ask if fish is okay, but it's not essential if you make sure she has plenty to eat.

Understood. If Carol isn't at the table, then gluten-free and no garlic or onion don't apply to Saturday's menu. I'll keep her out of the dinner constraints. If that changes and she ends up joining, let me know and we'll adjust, since no garlic or onion plus gluten-free is a real puzzle for most dishes.

It might also be worth confirming with your partner whether she's actually joining, just so you aren't surprised on the day. Otherwise, the dinner is still eight people: you, your partner, Priya, Marcus, Dana, Tomas, Wren, and Eli.

Easy fix: pick two wines, one white and one red, and don't overthink it. A crisp white like a Sauvignon Blanc or a dry Riesling goes with nearly everything. For red, a light to medium one like a Pinot Noir or a Côtes du Rhône is friendly and not too heavy. Add a sparkling option to greet people with, and a couple non-alcoholic choices like sparkling water with citrus.

Plan about one bottle per two people for wine, so for eight people, four to five bottles total is plenty. If someone asks you "what wine pairs with this?" you can just say "whatever you like!" and nobody will mind. A shop employee can also help if you tell them your budget and the meal.
ok 5 bottles. cool. back to the interview ugh. what if they ask about conflict with a coworker. i always blank on the behavioral stuff

Behavioral questions are way easier with a frame. Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Prepare maybe four stories you can reshape for different questions: a conflict, a failure you learned from, a time you led without authority, and a time you delivered under pressure.

For the conflict one, pick a real disagreement that was about the work and not personal. Describe how you listened to the other side, found the shared goal, and reached something workable. Avoid trashing the other person. Interviewers mainly want to see maturity and that you can disagree and still collaborate.

Do you have a story in mind? Even a rough one, I can help shape it.
kinda. theres this time a teammate and i disagreed about a migration approach and we ended up doing a spike on both and picking one with data. idk if thats good

That is a great story, actually. It shows you resolved a technical disagreement without ego by turning it into an experiment. Structure it like this: the situation (two valid approaches to the migration and a stalemate), the task (decide without damaging the relationship or stalling the project), the action (propose a time-boxed spike on each approach, agree on the criteria beforehand), and the result (chose one using the data, shipped on time, and the teammate felt heard).

If you can add a number, like the spike took two days or the chosen approach cut migration time by some percent, that makes it stronger. And end with what you learned, like "agree on how you'll decide before you start arguing."

Noted. For Tomas, keep the whole menu mild, or at least keep anything spicy completely separate and optional (and I'd lean toward skipping it altogether since you have so many other constraints). That includes black pepper in heavy amounts, chili flakes, hot sauces, jalapeños, and curry blends. Mild seasoning with herbs, citrus, garlic, and gentle spices is the way to go.

Running list: Marcus, tree nut allergy. Dana, no cilantro. Priya, no meat. Tomas, no spicy food. Wren and Eli are still unknown, so ask them if you can, but otherwise assume nothing unusual.

Good, that simplifies things. I'll treat Eli as eat-anything and Wren as probably fine, with a note that if you get a chance, a quick text to Wren would settle it. People sometimes forget to mention things until the food's in front of them.

So the core constraints are no tree nuts, no cilantro, no meat for Priya, and nothing spicy. That's very workable. Lots of good dinners fit all of that.

Gore-free and British, that narrows it in a fun way. Hot Fuzz has some gore, actually, so that's a mild caution; it's cartoonish but there are a couple of messy scenes. In Bruges has a bit too. If she's squeamish, better picks are Paddington 2, The Death of Stalin (dark funny, mostly not gory), Knives Out (British-adjacent cast and tone, little gore), or Four Weddings and a Funeral for something gentle.

For dumb funny and British without gore, I'd go Paddington 2 if you want something warm, or The Death of Stalin if you want sharp. Which feels more like a wrecked Sunday?

For a Saturday dinner, I'd say 6:30 or 7 for arrival, with food on the table around 7:30. That gives people time to arrive, grab a drink, and nibble on something. Tell them 7:00 and plan the main to come out at about 7:45. Guests rarely arrive on time exactly, and a bit of cushion saves you from the stress of watching the clock.

Work backward: if the main takes 90 minutes to cook, start by 6:00 at the latest, and do as much prep as possible Friday night and Saturday afternoon. Chopping, sauces, and desserts can all be done ahead.
7 it is. ok back to interview, they said theres a coding round too, like live. what should i practice

For a senior backend role at a freight company, live coding tends to be practical rather than puzzle-heavy. Practice problems involving intervals and scheduling (overlapping delivery windows), graphs and shortest path (routing), heaps and priority queues (assigning loads to carriers), and hash map based problems (grouping shipments). Also practice parsing and transforming messy data, since integrations with carriers often involve ugly inputs.

Talk out loud as you code, write a few test cases up front, and be ready to discuss complexity. If you get stuck, state the brute-force approach first, then improve it. Interviewers care a lot about your process.

Right, since he's not attending, his dairy allergy doesn't constrain your menu. The one thing worth checking is what's in the dessert he brings. Because of Marcus's tree nut allergy, ask your brother in law whether it contains any nuts. Dairy-free desserts very often use almond or cashew or coconut milk, and almond or cashew would be a problem. A quick message like "can you make sure it's nut-free, Marcus has a serious tree nut allergy?" should cover it. Or, to be safe, you could make your own dessert and skip his.

Good plan. Being direct is the kind option here, since an allergic reaction at your own dinner party is the thing you most want to avoid. If he's unsure about ingredients, the "don't bring it" backup is totally fair.

Meanwhile, you also have a lot of options for a nut-free dessert that everyone can eat. We can get to that when we do the menu. Do you want to start building the menu now, or keep chatting about the interview a bit longer?
ugh both. interview first one more thing, what do i ask THEM at the end. im always like uh no questions

Always have questions, since "no questions" can read as low interest. Good ones: "What does success look like in the first 90 days?" "How does the team handle on-call and incidents?" "What are the biggest technical challenges the platform is facing in the next year?" "How do engineers and operations folks work together?" and "What do you like most about working here?"

For a freight brokerage, a great domain question is "How do you balance automation with the human relationships between brokers, shippers, and carriers?" It shows you're thinking about the actual business.

love that last one. ok. so my partner just asked what i want for lunch and i said idk and she said "thats what you said yesterday" lol anyway. back to the menu. i wanna make something kinda impressive but not hard

Impressive but not hard: braises, sheet pan dishes, and big-batch baked pastas are the hosts' secret weapons, because they're mostly hands-off. The key is picking something that you can make mostly ahead and that is flexible enough to serve different dietary needs.

One smart structure for a mixed table is a "build your own" meal, where the base is something everyone can eat and the toppings or add-ons vary. For example, a big grain bowl or taco style spread where the meat is separate. Another is a main that's inherently vegetarian and hearty, with a separate protein for the meat-eaters.

Do you have a cuisine in mind, or any dishes you already know how to cook well?

Good, so you have real options. Let me think through each against what you've told me.

Roast chicken is a crowd pleaser but it doesn't work for Priya on its own. The curry is tricky because of Tomas and any cilantro garnish for Dana, though it's easily adjusted if you skip the heat and the cilantro. And the pesto is an interesting one: traditional pesto uses pine nuts and sometimes walnuts or almonds, so with Marcus's allergy, it's a risk unless you make a version with sunflower seeds or leave it nut-free entirely.

Pasta is the most flexible of the three. A big baked pasta or a mild sauce with a vegetarian option would work. Do you want me to suggest a couple of full menus built around your skills?

Understood, ignoring your sister's preferences entirely, since she's out of town and not attending. The list for Saturday stays the same: the eight people at the table are you, your partner, Priya, Marcus, Dana, Tomas, Wren, and Eli.

Ready for menu ideas whenever you are.

Good to know. Your partner doesn't like olives, which is easy to work around, and that one counts because she's at the table. It's a preference, not an allergy, so you could have olives as an optional side for others, but I'd keep them out of the main dishes to keep her happy. No need to apologize, your brain is juggling a lot. For a software role at a logistics company, a suit is almost certainly too much. Business casual is the safe move: a button-down or a nice sweater, clean chinos or dark jeans, and decent shoes. If it's remote, a clean shirt and tidy background are enough.

If you want to be safe, check the recruiter's note or the company's careers page photos. If everyone is in hoodies, go one step above hoodie. Dressing slightly nicer than the average employee is the usual rule.

Salary questions are awkward but there's a good way through it. First, try to deflect politely early on: "I'd like to learn more about the role and scope first, and I'm confident we can find a number that works. Can you share the range for this position?" Many places will share the range, and in some states they're legally required to post it.

If you do have to give a number, base it on market data for senior backend roles in your area and give a range where the bottom is a number you'd be genuinely happy with. Don't anchor on your current salary. If you want, tell me the general market you're in and I can help you think about a range.
ill figure it out later. brain full. gimme the dinner menus finally lol

Here are three directions, each built to be easy to scale for eight:

1. Baked pasta night. A big pan of baked ziti with a mild tomato and basil sauce and mozzarella, plus a separate tray of roasted vegetables for Priya, a green salad with a nut-free vinaigrette, and garlic bread (no nuts, no spice). Dessert: lemon olive oil cake or a simple fruit crisp using oats and butter, nut-free.

2. Mediterranean spread. Roast chicken with lemon and herbs on one tray, a separate tray of roasted vegetables and chickpeas for Priya, rice pilaf, tzatziki or hummus (check labels for nuts and avoid any cilantro), and a simple salad. Dessert: panna cotta with berries.

3. Mild vegetable curry plus chicken. A coconut-based curry without heat, served with rice and flatbread, with a roasted chicken option on the side. Skip chili and cilantro. Note that coconut is generally not considered a tree nut allergen for most people but some people avoid it, so ask Marcus.

I can adjust any of these when we finalize. Which feels closest to you?

i like the baked pasta one but the roast chicken is more impressive maybe? idk. also i was gonna do a big charcuterie board to start with because i bought a bunch of stuff already. like salami, cheeses, a jar of spicy pepper jelly, some crackers, and mixed nuts and olives because they were on sale lol. is that ok

Charcuterie is a great starter, but several of those items need attention given your guest list. Salami won't work for Priya, so make sure there are plenty of cheeses, crackers, and fruit that she can eat. The spicy pepper jelly is a problem for Tomas, so I'd either skip it or put out a mild jam instead, like fig or apricot. The mixed nuts are the big one: with Marcus's tree nut allergy, I'd keep those out of the house for the evening, or at least entirely out of the party area, and also check whether your crackers were made in a facility with nuts or contain any seed or nut flour. Olives are fine for everyone except maybe your partner, who doesn't love them, so a small bowl is okay.

So: keep the salami, cheeses, fruit, crackers (check labels), a mild jam, and a small bowl of olives. Drop the mixed nuts and the spicy jelly.
ugh ok yeah no nuts. i'll put the nuts away and not use them. good catch. wait does cross contamination matter if i use the same cutting board

It can, for a true allergy. Trace amounts of the allergen on a board, knife, or serving utensil can be enough to cause a reaction in a sensitive person. If you cut or handled nuts recently, wash the board, knife, and any serving dishes thoroughly with hot soapy water, or use a fresh board. Also avoid serving utensils that have touched the nut containers.

For a party, the easiest approach is to keep nuts entirely out of the kitchen on Saturday, put the bag in a closed container in the garage or a cabinet, and use clean tools for everything. Wipe counters down before you start prepping. That level of care is plenty.

Yes, here's a rough shape that keeps the pressure spread out:

Wednesday: light interview prep in the evening. Do two or three interval or scheduling coding problems and rehearse your STAR stories out loud. Text Wren and confirm Eli and Wren have no restrictions if you decide to.

Thursday: interview day. Eat something, do a short warm-up problem in the morning, and keep the evening free so you can rest. Maybe do a quick debrief note of what you'd improve.

Friday: grocery shop in the morning or after work. Do prep in the evening: chop vegetables, make sauces, and bake dessert. Watch The Lady Vanishes after.

Saturday: cook the main in the afternoon, set the table by 5, and have drinks ready. Guests at 7.

kinda lol. what about cleaning. my place is a disaster

Do the cleaning in zones so it doesn't take over. Focus on what guests will actually see and use: the entryway, the living room, the dining area, the bathroom, and the kitchen. Skip bedrooms and anything behind a closed door.

Do a big declutter on Thursday night or Friday, then on Saturday morning just wipe surfaces, vacuum, and clean the bathroom. Put a fresh hand towel out, a candle or some soft lighting, and a trash bag ready for dishes. Dim lights and a playlist hide a lot of mess honestly.

A good answer follows the incident lifecycle: detect, mitigate, communicate, resolve, and learn. Say something like: "First priority is to restore service, even if it's a temporary mitigation like rolling back a deploy or failing over. I make sure stakeholders are updated regularly so they aren't guessing. After it's stable, we do a blameless postmortem to find root causes and put in actions so it doesn't repeat."

For freight, mention the impact of downtime: late loads, missed pickups, and customers who can't see their shipments. And if you have a real example from your reliability work, use it.

That's a strong example, especially with the numbers. Frame it as: the pipeline broke and blocked about 200 engineers, you took the lead on triage, found the cause, applied a mitigation, communicated status to the affected teams, then drove a follow-up so it wouldn't happen again. Add the lesson, like adding better monitoring or a safer rollout process for pipeline changes.

For a logistics company, you can connect it: "I treat internal tools like production systems because the downstream cost of downtime is high," which maps well to a world where downtime means delayed freight.

Classic flaky-test situation. Passes locally, fails intermittently on CI usually means one of a few things: a race between async work and your assertion, state leaking between tests, or an environment difference between your laptop and CI. Can you paste the test and tell me what the CI failure message looks like? Even a rough description of the error helps. Also tell me roughly how the monorepo runs jest, whether it's one root config or per-package configs.

If you're using `getByText` right after triggering a refresh, that's a likely suspect, and `findByText` or `waitFor` would handle the async gap. Different symptom, and that one smells like mock leakage between tests, not async timing. If `jest.spyOn(...)` is set up in one test and never restored or cleared, call counts accumulate across tests in the same file. The "received 3" suggests two earlier tests also called the spied function and the counter wasn't reset. Check whether you have `clearMocks`, `resetMocks`, or `restoreMocks` in the jest config, or an `afterEach(() => jest.clearAllMocks())` in the file.

On CI, the full file runs and other tests' calls pile up. Add `afterEach(() => { jest.clearAllMocks(); })` or set `clearMocks: true` in the package's jest config. Better still, use `restoreMocks: true` if you want spies restored to the originals too.

That's the "not wrapped in act(...)" warning from React Testing Library. It usually means a state update happened outside of the test's awareness, such as a timer or a promise resolving after the test already moved on. It's often a warning, not a failure, unless your setup makes console errors fail the test (some repos do that with a jest setup file). Does your setup file turn console.error into a thrown error?

That is a good practice for keeping a codebase clean, but it makes async leakage obvious. For "shows spinner then table," make sure the test awaits the final state before it ends, e.g. `await screen.findByRole('table')`, or `await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByRole('progressbar'))`. If the test ends while the fetch is still pending, the later resolution triggers a state update after the test is over, and that's the act warning. Make sure the last line of the test awaits something that only appears after the update.

It's the timezone thing you mentioned earlier. This isn't flaky at all, it's deterministic, and none of the earlier mock/await stuff has anything to do with it.

`toLocaleString()` with no `timeZone` option renders in whatever zone the process is running in:

- **Your laptop (US Central, CDT = UTC-5):** `2026-11-01T03:30:00Z` → **Oct 31, 10:30 PM**
- **CI (`TZ=UTC` in the workflow env):** same instant → **Nov 1, 3:30 AM**

Those are exactly your Expected and Received. Priya's expected string was produced on a Central-time machine (hers or yours), so the test passes for anyone in Central and fails anywhere else, every time. And she picked a timestamp that crosses midnight, so the zone even changes the *day*, which is why it looks so wrong. (DST ending Nov 1 doesn't matter here, it's still CDT at 03:30Z.)

**Fix: make the test independent of the machine's timezone.** Two ways to do it:

1. **Pin the zone where the date gets formatted** (best if the component should show a specific zone):
   ```ts
   date.toLocaleString('en-US', { timeZone: 'America/Chicago', dateStyle: 'medium', timeStyle: 'short' })
   ```
   Or, if the component deliberately uses the user's local zone, keep it as is and fix the test instead (option 2).

2. **Pin TZ for the whole jest run** so laptops behave like CI. In billing-ui's jest config, add a `globalSetup` that does `process.env.TZ = 'UTC'`. Then change the expected value to `"Nov 1, 2026, 3:30 AM"`. Do it in globalSetup, not in a test file, because by then Node may already have cached the zone.

I'd go with 2 at minimum, and also pin `'en-US'` while you're in there. That's the same locale bug your teammate hit with the date range picker. To be honest, this is also why I said to pin timezone there too: that one only passed because everybody running it happened to be in the same zone.

You can confirm it in 5 seconds locally: `TZ=UTC npx jest InvoiceTable` should fail on your laptop the same way CI does.

It's a work repo, so put this up as a PR and maybe tag Priya so she knows why it broke.

Nice, April is a great window for the Southwest. It's warm enough for the desert but mostly before the brutal summer heat. Starting from Albuquerque gives you a lot of options. A common loop is Albuquerque to Flagstaff, then up to the Grand Canyon or Page and Antelope Canyon, over to Monument Valley, into Moab for Arches and Canyonlands, and then back down through the Four Corners area to Albuquerque.

For 9 or 10 days, I'd think about 4 or 5 big anchor stops instead of trying to see everything. Do you two want more hiking, more scenic driving, or more food and weird roadside stuff? That changes the route a lot.

That's Horseshoe Bend, near Page, Arizona. It's an easy walk of about 1.5 miles round trip from the parking lot, and it's best in late afternoon or around sunset when the light is softer, though it gets crowded. There's a parking fee per vehicle, so check the current price before you go.

Since you're already near Page, you could pair it with Antelope Canyon, but those slot canyons require a guided tour on Navajo land, so book ahead. April tours can sell out weeks in advance.

Do you know where your own property corner pins are? Sometimes you can find them with a metal detector, and your county recorder or assessor's office may have your plat on file.

If it does turn out to be over the line, you have options ranging from a friendly conversation, to a mediated agreement, to a formal survey. A licensed surveyor usually costs a few hundred dollars up to over a thousand depending on lot size and area, but it's definitive.

Congrats on starting, and the finger pain is totally normal. For the first few weeks your fingertips are building callouses, and it's usually the worst around weeks two to four. Short, frequent sessions are better than one long painful one. Even 10 to 15 minutes twice a day will help more than an hour on the weekend.

What guitar are you playing, acoustic or electric? And what are you using to learn, lessons, YouTube, an app?

The FG800 is a great pick for a beginner, and a used one for $150 is a good deal. Justin's Grade 1 is a solid path.

On the F chord, almost everyone struggles with it. Many teachers suggest starting with a simplified version, often called the mini F, where you only play the top four strings and don't fully barre. Then you work up to the full barre over weeks or months. Also check your guitar's action, the string height. If the strings are high, barre chords are much harder, and a quick setup at a guitar shop is usually cheap.
