You're right. Zion is a big detour from Albuquerque, roughly 9 hours of driving back. Options: drop Zion and swap in Capitol Reef, which is much closer to the Moab side. Or fly out of a different city, like Las Vegas or Salt Lake City, and do a one-way rental, though that often adds a drop fee.

If you drop Zion, you can do a Moab to Capitol Reef to Bryce day, and then loop back south. Capitol Reef also has a lot of quiet, less crowded hiking.
ok I like dropping zion, crowds make me anxious anyway. what about food in moab tho, teo is gonna ask. I heard about some taco place?

Moab has a lot of casual spots. Without knowing exactly which one you heard about, there are a few well-known ones, like Moab Garage Co for coffee and breakfast, Quesadilla Mobilla, which is a food truck, and Moab Brewery for a bigger sit-down meal. Moab also has lots of food trucks.

I'd double-check hours because many places keep reduced or seasonal hours in April. If the taco place you remember had a name, send it and I can help narrow it down.
it was like Quesa something yeah probably that one lol. ugh ok Gary update, he waved at me today like nothing happened. like bro. I stood there with my coffee and just stared

Passive-aggressive friendliness is its own kind of awkward. You don't owe a big reaction, though. A neutral nod is fine while you're sorting out the facts. If you decide to get the survey, a calm, short note works well: "Hey, I'd like to confirm the line, can you send the survey you mentioned? If not, I'm going to have mine done."

That keeps you from being the aggressor and gives him a chance to resolve it.

i like that. maybe i'll text him that. or leave a note. idk. i hate texting him cuz then he has my number lmao he already does though, we did a block party thing. anyway guitar again, I tried the mini F for like twenty min and my finger still hurts. also my wife says I play the same three chords constantly and its driving her nuts

Three chords on repeat is actually a good sign, that's how muscle memory builds, but your wife has a point. You can keep the practice productive and less annoying by chaining them into songs. With Em, A, and D, plus a G, you can play a surprising number of songs. Knockin' on Heaven's Door is G, D, Am, and C, which is a common beginner song.

Also try practicing with a timer: five minutes of chord changes, five minutes of a song, five minutes of something fun. Short blocks help you stay focused and keep the sessions from feeling like a chore.
ok I can do knockin on heavens door lol thats like the first song everyone learns. wait I just remembered, we need to figure out where to stay. teo wants to camp but I'm like 40 and my back says no

Totally fair. A mix could work. Camp one or two nights in the really scenic places, like near Capitol Reef or Monument Valley, and book cheap motels or Airbnbs for the rest. Nights in places like Moab and Page tend to book up in spring, so reserve those early.

Car camping in an Outback is also decent. You can fold down the back seats, use a sleeping pad, and avoid a tent entirely. Bring layers because desert nights in April can drop into the 30s.

oh shit the nights get that cold?? ok yeah I'd need a real sleeping bag. I have one from like 2009 idk if it still works. so Capitol Reef camping. is there a hot spring around there or something, someone mentioned hot springs

There are some warm springs in the broader region, but not directly at Capitol Reef. Hot springs in Utah are more commonly found farther west, near places like Monroe or Midway. In Arizona and New Mexico, there are more options, like Jemez Springs in New Mexico, which is close to your Albuquerque start and could be a nice first or last day stop.

If you want, I can look into a soak near the beginning or end of the trip so your muscles get a break after all the hiking.
ooh jemez springs on the last day sounds perfect. ok ok. what about Monument Valley, is it hard to get around

Monument Valley is on Navajo Tribal Park land, and the main attraction is the 17-mile Valley Drive, a gravel road you can do in your own vehicle, though it can be rough. An Outback should handle it. You can also book a guided tour, which gets you to places the self-drive loop doesn't reach.

Camping is available at the park's campground, and there's also a lodge, The View Hotel, though it's pricey and books early.
hmm the view hotel, nah too pricey probably. I wonder if Goulding's is cheaper. teo said somethin about a trading post too

Goulding's Lodge is nearby, and it's often a bit more affordable than The View, but prices vary a lot by season. The trading post is likely Goulding's Trading Post, which has a small museum tied to the old John Ford westerns. There's also Twin Arrows Trading Post along I-40 between Flagstaff and Winslow, which is a quirky roadside stop with a couple of big painted arrows.

For weird roadside stuff, that Flagstaff to Winslow stretch of Route 66 is great. You can stand on a corner in Winslow, Arizona, as the song goes.
lmao standing on the corner in winslow, I can play take it easy?? it's like G and C and D, i think. is that real

Yes, that's real. Take It Easy is mostly built on G, C, and D, with some other chords like Em and Am depending on the version. The strumming pattern is a little tricky, but a simplified version with those chords is a nice beginner goal, and standing on that corner in Winslow while playing it would be a very fitting photo.

Bring the guitar, if you want. A small travel guitar would be easier than the full FG800, though.

bringing the guitar on the trip, huh, teo would hate it lmao he'd be like we have no room. ok idk. back to the fence for a sec. my wife found the plat map online and says the lot lines are like 7 feet from my driveway edge but I measured and the fence is 6ft 4 from my driveway

That's useful. If the plat map is accurate and the driveway edge is the reference, then the fence would be about 8 inches onto your side. But a plat map is a general document and can be off from the real survey. Also, the driveway edge may not be exactly where the plat assumes. I'd treat it as evidence rather than proof.

Taking photos and a measuring-tape record is still worthwhile. If the numbers hold up with the pin locations, you'll have a strong case in conversation.
ok so 8 inches. thats what i said, 6 inches was a guess lol. so Im basically right. I'm gonna put that in my text to Gary. maybe. or maybe I let it go idk. i hate conflict but it also pisses me off

Understandable. Letting it go is a legitimate choice, but be aware of a couple of things. In some places, if you don't object for a long enough period, it can weaken your position later, especially with things like adverse possession or boundary by acquiescence. The time frames are usually many years, and they vary by state, so it's not an immediate risk.

Either way, writing down the date you first raised the issue and keeping the text or note record is cheap insurance.
ok yeah. i'll do the survey after the trip maybe. gotta save money for the trip lol. which reminds me I should look at what flights cost, and the rental. ok whats a rough budget for 10 days, two guys

A rough breakdown for two people, split evenly, might look like this. Flights vary hugely, so I'll leave them out. Rental car with insurance might be $600 to $900 for 10 days. Gas, with the mileage of this loop, maybe $300 to $400. Lodging, mixing camping and motels, maybe $500 to $900 each over the trip. Food, $40 to $70 per person per day. Park fees, an America the Beautiful pass for $80 covers most national parks and is worth it if you hit three or more.

So roughly $1,500 to $2,500 per person excluding flights, depending on how nice you want it.

damn ok. the park pass thing is smart, we'd do arches, capitol reef, canyonlands, maybe grand canyon. oh also wait should we do Bryce? i feel like everyone says bryce is sick but its like 4 hours from moab

Bryce is stunning, with all those hoodoos, and the sunrise from Sunset Point or Bryce Point is the classic photo. The drive from Moab is a bit over 4 hours, but if you route Moab to Capitol Reef to Bryce, then back toward Page via Kanab, it's a natural arc and breaks up the driving.

With 10 days, I'd rank it behind Arches and Capitol Reef but ahead of a second Arizona stop, if you want to cut something.
ok bryce stays maybe. teo says it's cold there in april tho, like snow. ok whatever. quick guitar thing, how do i know if my guitar needs a setup? the strings feel like theyre far from the neck

A simple check is to press a string down at the first fret and at the fret where the neck meets the body, often around the 12th to 14th fret. The gap between the string and the fret in the middle should be small. If you see a big gap, it's likely high action.

A shop will measure and adjust the truss rod and the saddle height, often for $50 to $80. With a $150 used guitar, that's worth it and will make chords like F much more doable.
ok I'll take it to a shop, theres one near me called Hot Cross Strings. oh also I've been thinking a lot about getting a capo. is that cheating

Not cheating at all. A capo is a normal tool used by professionals, and for beginners it can make certain songs easier to play in a comfortable key. It also helps you match the key of a song to your voice. A basic capo is around $10 to $15, so it's a cheap buy.

Just don't use it as a crutch to avoid learning the open chords you need. Using it for some songs and not others keeps your skills growing.

lol ok. so anyway Teo texted again and wants to add Santa Fe at the start cuz he wants to eat at this place called Cafe Pasqual's. I have no opinion on that. but also I just realized he said we'd be in albuquerque the first night, so santa fe would be like an hour north, ok?

Yes, Santa Fe is about an hour north of Albuquerque. It could be an easy first day: pick up the car, drive up, have a nice meal, and spend the night. The next morning you would head west, but that adds some distance on day two, since you'd be going back through Albuquerque or taking a northern route toward Four Corners.

If Teo's heart is set on that restaurant, I'd consider trading it for the last day, since Santa Fe could close the loop and you could soak at Jemez Springs on the way.

hmm that's actually smart, end in santa fe and jemez. save the fancy meal for last. ok ok. I'm making a list in my notes app. so far: horseshoe bend, antelope canyon tour, monument valley, arches, capitol reef, maybe bryce, sedona, jemez springs, santa fe. thats a lot of stuff lol

It's a lot, but it's workable if you keep drive days short. A few places you can cut if time runs tight: Sedona, since you can do it as a quick morning stop or skip it, and Bryce. The must-dos seem to be Arches, Capitol Reef, Monument Valley, and Horseshoe Bend.

Do you want me to estimate drive times between each stop so you can see the daily mileage?

yeah but later. my brain is fried lol. ok gary thing, my wife says she wants to just bake him cookies and kill him with kindness and I'm like NO. we are not baking cookies for a man who stole 8 inches of our land

Ha. There's a middle path between cookies and war. You can be polite and firm at the same time. The cookie plan might work if the goal is to keep neighbors on good terms, but it doesn't solve the boundary question. I'd handle the fence issue separately and plainly, then be friendly about other things.

Maybe you let your wife do the cookies for the holidays, and you do the paperwork.

lmao "you do the paperwork" ok. fine. she can bake and I'll do the survey. I swear if he goes full HOA on me. wait is he allowed to paint it? cuz he mentioned staining the fence side facing me and I'm like why would that be his call

Generally, the finished side of a fence versus the structural side can matter. Some local ordinances require the "good side" face outward toward the neighbor. If the fence is on your land, even partly, you might have a say. If it's on his land, he can usually stain it however he wants, though local codes and HOA rules, if any, may apply.

Since there's a boundary question, I'd hold off on arguing about the stain until you know where the line is.

ok that's fair. the survey is gonna settle everything. unless it says hes right, then Im gonna look like an idiot lol. 600 bucks to be wrong. ok so back to the trip and the car. should we get the outback or do we need a bigger suv for the gravel roads in monument valley

An Outback has decent ground clearance, about 8.7 inches, and all-wheel drive, so for Valley Drive in good conditions it's fine. Check your rental agreement though, because many rental companies prohibit driving on unpaved roads, which can affect your insurance coverage. That's a real thing to read before you go.

If you plan to do any serious dirt road driving, like in Capitol Reef's Notom-Bullfrog Road or Canyonlands' Needles district, a high clearance vehicle helps, and paved routes still cover the highlights.

oh damn the unpaved road thing, good catch. maybe we book a guided tour for the valley so the car isn't at risk. wait hold on, I wanna ask something about capitol reef, is it true theres pies? someone told me you can buy pie there

Yes. At Capitol Reef there's a historic Fruita area with orchards, and the Gifford Homestead sells fresh baked fruit pies, usually from spring through fall. They're small hand pies and they sell out on busy days, so earlier is better. It's a well-loved stop, so putting it on the list makes sense.

Orchard fruit is also free to pick in season in some areas, though April is probably too early for most of it.

pie!! ok teo's gonna lose his mind. the gifford thing, ok adding it. oh also, Capitol Reef is near Torrey and there's this cafe there, Cafe Diablo, that teo found on yelp, it has some wild reviews for the lamb shank

Cafe Diablo is a popular upscale-ish spot in Torrey with a Southwestern menu, and it gets good reviews for dishes like the lamb shank. It can fill up in the evening, so a reservation is wise, and it might have limited hours in early spring. Check their site close to your dates.

Torrey is also a good base for Capitol Reef, with a handful of motels and small restaurants.

ok so food list is: chuckwagon in page, quesa-whatever in moab, gifford pie at capitol reef, cafe diablo in torrey, cafe pasquals in santa fe. oh and obviously the diner thing. wow thats a lot of food stops. teo will be thrilled

That's a great food list. The route as it stands gives you a good variety: biscuits in Page, tacos in Moab, pie and a nice dinner near Capitol Reef, and a splurge in Santa Fe. If you're going to be in the Hanksville and Capitol Reef region anyway, you'll want to work out the timing for that breakfast stop.

Do you want me to figure out where it falls in your drive?
yeah maybe later, I'm so tired of planning rn lol. let me think about guitar instead. ive been practicing the mini F for a week and I can sorta do it, but it buzzes. why does it buzz

Buzzing usually means a string isn't pressed firmly enough or isn't touching the fret right. Common causes are your finger being too far from the fret wire, which means you want to press closer to the fret rather than in the middle of the space; not enough pressure; or another finger accidentally touching an adjacent string.

Also, if your guitar has high action or a fret issue, that can cause buzzing, so the setup is worth doing. Try playing each string one at a time to find which one is buzzing.
ok it's the high e string. my index finger's knuckle is touching it prolly. I'll try to curl my finger more

That's a very common culprit. Your index finger should be rolled slightly onto its side, so the bony part rather than the fleshy pad is doing the work for the mini barre, and the knuckle should be clear of the thin strings. Try slowly rolling the finger toward the thumb and see if the high E rings clean. It takes a little while to find the angle that works.

Record yourself on your phone. You'll often spot what's going on better than you'd feel it.

ok will do. ugh. ok so ive been thinking about the fence and maybe I'm overreacting, but this morning Gary was out there with a drill adding more screws to the fence panels on MY side. like on the side facing me. and I swear he was looking at me like a little smug

Even if he's just maintaining the fence, I understand why it felt loaded. If the fence is partly on your property, his working on the side facing you isn't automatically a problem, and it may be nothing more than routine upkeep. But it's one more reason to get the line confirmed so you aren't stewing over ambiguous moments.

Keep it factual and don't let the smugness, real or imagined, drive your decisions.

you're right. ok, deep breath. i'll call the survey place monday. wait it's thursday so I'd have to wait. ok. anyway one more trip question, what do i do about the sleeping bag. should I just buy a new one

If your bag is from 2009 and has been stored compressed, the insulation may have lost loft, which reduces warmth. Lay it out and fluff it, and check for any damaged zippers. A bag rated at 20 degrees Fahrenheit is a safe choice for April nights in the high desert. REI and similar stores often have decent options in the $100 to $150 range.

You could also rent a bag if you only camp a few nights.

ok I'll just check REI. the april trip is still like 5 months out so no rush. oh my god, I just realized the date, thats not 5 months, wait what month is it now, it's november so april is like 5 months yeah ok fine

Right, November to April is about five months, so you have plenty of time. The main things to book early are Antelope Canyon, anywhere you want to sleep in Page and Moab, and Arches timed entry if it's required for your dates, since that program has changed over the years.

The rest can stay flexible, which suits you.
timed entry for arches?? ugh. ok. what a pain. fine I'll look at it in like february. also I think I wanna get a travel guitar like a Martin Backpacker or whatever, you think that's dumb or good

It isn't dumb, but I'd think twice. A Backpacker has a short scale and a different feel from your FG800, and it can make switching back and forth slightly awkward when you're a beginner. It also sounds a bit boxy. If you want to keep practicing on the road, a small parlor guitar, or just a few finger exercises with a practice device, could work.

But honestly, with Teo already skeptical about space, you might just skip it for a ten day trip and come back with fresh fingers.

lol fresh fingers. no I don't think so, my callouses would die. ok I'll think about it. oh whoa, something just came to mind, my cousin said the hot springs near Hanksville aren't actually hot springs, theyre just warm and gross. idk if that's true

I can't verify that specific place without more detail, but warm natural pools can vary a lot in temperature and cleanliness. Some are well-maintained and some are more like muddy seeps. A good habit is to check recent reviews and land management pages before you go, since conditions can change from season to season, and access can be tricky on dirt roads.

Jemez Springs at the end of your trip is a more reliable soak, with developed options.
ok jemez it is. so wait, final recap on the route? I wanna know the order of stuff cuz I keep jumbling it in my head

Here's a clean version of the loop based on what we've talked about. Albuquerque start, then west to Flagstaff, with a quick Sedona stop if you want it. Then north to Page for Horseshoe Bend and the Antelope Canyon tour. Next Monument Valley, then up to Moab for Arches and Canyonlands. From Moab you go to Hanksville and Capitol Reef, with Torrey as a base, then optionally Bryce, though that's the one to cut if time is tight. Then back south and east toward New Mexico, ending with Jemez Springs and Santa Fe.

That's about ten days with some tight spots. We can refine the mileage whenever you want.
ok that's actually a good order. thanks. I'm gonna go practice, wife is out so I can be loud lol. mini F here I come

Have fun, and remember the short-session rule: ten focused minutes beats an hour of frustration. Keep your wrist relaxed and let the finger roll do the work. Come back anytime and we can pick the trip back up, mileage and all.

ok I'm back lol, practiced for like 40 min which is probably too long cuz my fingertips feel like hot dogs. but I got the mini F clean like 3 times in a row!! then I lost it again. ok also I started thinking about the trip while I was playing and I realized I never asked about water and shit, like do we need to carry a ton of water in the desert or is that a movie thing, I feel like Teo is gonna overpack and make me carry it all

Congrats on the clean mini F, that's real progress, and the hot dog fingertips will toughen up. Rest them a bit tomorrow if they're sore.

On water, it's not a movie thing. In the desert you lose water faster than you notice because the air is so dry. A common guideline for hiking is about a liter per person for every couple of hours, more in the heat, and in April you can still get warm afternoons in the 70s and 80s. For the car, a big jug or two of backup water is smart, especially on long stretches with no services, like between Hanksville and other small towns. For trails, carry what you need plus a margin, and have a plan for electrolytes if you sweat a lot.

You don't need to carry a crazy amount on every hike, but Teo's instinct to overpack water isn't bad, it's just that you should divide the weight fairly.

ok fair, Ill carry half and he carries half lol. also gas, are there places where theres just no gas for like 100 miles, someone said that about utah and it freaked me out. tbh Im the kind of person that lets the tank go down to like a quarter before I even think about it, my wife hates it

Your wife has a point for this trip. Parts of southern Utah and northern Arizona have long gaps between stations, and some of the small ones have limited hours or close early. A good rule is to fill up whenever you're at half a tank and you see a station, especially before heading into stretches like Highway 24 through Capitol Reef country, or the drive across the Navajo Nation.

Also download offline maps before you leave because cell service drops out in lots of the places you're planning to visit. It makes the long gaps a lot less stressful.

ugh ok half a tank rule, fine. offline maps, ok. one more fence thing and then I'll shut up, I found my dad's metal detector and put new batteries in, and it works!! I went out in the yard and got a beep near the back corner like 8 inches from where the fence is, so I think I found a pin. I didn't dig it up tho cuz I'm scared I'd mess it up

Nice find. Your instinct not to dig is a good one. Disturbing a survey monument can be a legal problem in many places, and it can invalidate the evidence you're trying to use. Mark the spot with a flag or a small stake, take photos, and measure from it to the fence and a fixed object like the corner of your house.

That gives you more than the plat map: a possible pin position. When you hire the surveyor, mention it. They'll confirm whether it's a real monument and where the line actually runs.
ok marking it with a pink flag from the garage lol. gary's gonna see it and freak. ok that's it, I'm good for tonight. I'll come back when I wanna lock in the trip stuff

Sounds good. The pink flag is a smart, low-key way to keep the spot safe, and it's hard to argue with a photo of a pin you found yourself. Enjoy the practice, and whenever you're ready we can lock in the route, the bookings that need to happen early, and the drive times between stops.

tests.title: Which run won
tests.trap: A data leak was found midway, and two scores were corrected. Espresso numbers everywhere.
tests.question: ok so after all that bs which run actually won and what lr was it, like the real one not the leaky one
turns: ok so I finally got the first fine tune finished last night and idk what to make of it lol. I called it run-a, its Llama 3.2 1B with lora, lr was 2e-4, and it got 71.4 on my eval set. is that good or

71.4 on its own doesn't tell you much without a baseline. What was the base model scoring on the same eval before you tuned it? If the untuned Llama 3.2 1B was sitting around 55 or 60, then 71.4 is a real jump. If it was already at 68, you've mostly burned a night of GPU time. Also worth knowing how big the eval set is, because on a few hundred examples a point or two is basically noise.

base was like 58.something I think. eval is 1000 examples, I made it myself from the slang convo stuff I scraped. ok good so its a real jump then. anyway bo woke up at 3:40 again this morning and I am DEAD

hes 2 and a bit. he wakes up and screams for like 40 min then goes back down. sooo fun. we moved bedtime to 7:15 from 7:45 cause someone online said overtired kids wake more but idk if its working, only been 3 nights

Three nights is too short to judge, especially with a regression going on. The overtired theory is real, though. Kids who go to bed too late often wake more in the night and early in the morning because their stress hormones are up. Give the earlier bedtime at least a week and keep everything else boring and consistent. Also check the nap. At two, a nap that runs past about 3:30 can push bedtime resistance and fragment the night.

Sour usually means under-extracted. 27 seconds for a 1 to 2 ratio isn't crazy, but sour says you want more extraction. Go finer first. Drop the grind a couple of notches, say to 12, keep the dose at 18g and the yield at 36g, and see if the shot time stretches into the low 30s. Change only one thing at a time or you won't know what fixed it.

ok going to 12 tomorrow. oh also I started run-b. same Llama 3.2 1B but I lowered lr way down to 5e-5 cause I read lower is more stable. uses the new bigger dataset I put together, v2, its got like 3x the data

Sounds like a good controlled-ish experiment, except you changed two things, the learning rate and the dataset. If run-b beats run-a you won't know which change did it. That's fine for a hobby project if you just want a better model, but if you want to learn something, you'd want one run that changes only lr on v1 data. How did the v2 dataset get built, by the way? Same scraping pipeline?
yeah same pipeline basically, I just scraped more subreddits and merged it with v1 and ran my dedup script. ok run-b finished and holy shit 78.9. thats a huge jump from 71.4!!

That is a big jump, 7.5 points. Before celebrating too hard, I'd sanity check one thing: since v2 was merged from more sources, make sure none of the eval examples ended up in the training data. yeah yeah I'll check that later. bo update: last night he slept through til 5:50!! so maybe the earlier bedtime is working?? or maybe he's just tired from the park lol

5:50 is a huge improvement over 3:40. One good night doesn't make a trend, but it's encouraging. Park days with lots of running and fresh air do help sleep a lot, so it could be a mix. Keep logging the wake times for a week or so and you'll see whether it holds.
also random but how do I know if lora rank matters. I used rank 16 and alpha 32 on everything cause some blog said so, 3 epochs, batch size 8. should I be tuning those too or is lr the main thing

Learning rate is usually the most sensitive knob, so you're right to start there. Rank and alpha matter too, but for a model this small and a task like slang understanding, rank 16 is a perfectly reasonable default. If you want a second experiment later, try rank 8 versus 32 with everything else frozen. Epochs matter as well: 3 epochs on a small dataset can overfit, so keep an eye on whether eval loss turns upward in the last epoch.

eval loss was still going down at the end of epoch 3 for run-a so I think its fine. ok espresso detour. my machine has a pid thing and I set the temp to 93 celsius. should it be higher for lighter roasts? the beans are a medium from the local place, says notes of caramel and hazelnut

Fair enough, but I'd bump it up the list, because "same threads" is exactly how overlap happens. It's a ten minute check: hash each eval example, hash each training example, and count matches. Do it before you trust any score from a run trained on v2.

74.2. so better than a but worse than b. so b is still the king

Take your 1000 eval examples and check how many appear in v2 exactly, and ideally also near-duplicates by normalizing case and punctuation. ok ran it. 312 of the 1000 eval examples are in v2, exact matches. 312!! thats awful. and v1? I checked v1 too and zero overlap, v1 was built before I merged the new stuff so its clean

So v1 is clean and v2 has a 31 percent leak. That means runs b and d, which trained on v2, were partially graded on material they'd already seen, so their scores are inflated. Runs a and c trained on v1 and are unaffected, so 71.4 and 74.2 stand. To get honest numbers for b and d, the cleanest option is to remove those 312 examples from v2, or simply evaluate on the 688 non-leaked eval examples. Which do you want to do?
just eval on the 688 clean ones, way faster than retraining. redoing b and d scores now. brb

Sounds good. One thing to keep in mind: the 688-example subset might be slightly easier or harder than the full 1000, so for a fair comparison you should also rescore runs a and c on the same 688. They shouldn't change much, but it keeps the table apples to apples.

right right. footnote lol. I'm gonna put "leaked, do not use" next to them

yeah. hmm. is it dumb that im this invested in this lol. like its a 1b model for slang

Based on run-e, cleaned v2 at 1e-4 gets 72.9, which is about 1.3 below v1 at the same lr, so the data effect may be around that size. That would suggest 5e-5 on v2 costs about another 1.5 or so compared to 1e-4, but that's inference rather than measurement. The only way to know is to run 5e-5 on v1.
ok I'll queue run-f, v1 data, lr 5e-5, and run-g at 5e-4 on v1. gonna start them tonight. they take like 2 hrs each so tomorrow I'll have em

Sounds good. Since you're running two at once, make sure they write checkpoints and logs to separate folders so they don't overwrite each other, and tag each with its lr and dataset in the name. After the leak, you'll want your results table to carry a column for which dataset and eval subset each score was computed on.
lol I'm putting in a data column. wait actually. the gpu only fits one at a time. so I'm just running f tonight and g tomorrow night

That works. Run-f first makes sense, because it fills the gap in your v1 curve and tells you whether lower lr is better or not. If run-f beats 74.2, you've got a new leader. If it doesn't, 1e-4 is probably your sweet spot, and run-g becomes more of a curiosity.
ok run-f is done, 73.1 on the eval, v1 data, 5e-5. so lower than c lol. so 1e-4 is the sweet spot probably

That fits a sweet spot near 1e-4: 2e-4 gives 71.4, 1e-4 gives 74.2, and 5e-5 gives 73.1. It's a nice smooth hill shape on v1, and all three are on clean data, so you can trust the comparison. Is run-g still planned for tomorrow night?
yeah run-g tomorrow. ok bo did the quiet time thing and it worked! he lay in his bed with books for an hour and then slept at 7:20. 6:20 wake. im so happy

That's great news. Quiet time with books is a nice middle path, and it respects that he's dropping the nap without making him overtired. Keep bedtime around 7:15 to 7:30 and you may have this settled. Regressions rarely end all at once, but this sounds like a real turn.
and espresso is going good too. ethiopian at 11 grind is dialed. I'm just gonna use 13 for the medium stuff. ok run-g finished. 5e-4 on v1 got 62.0. a cliff lol. so basically 1e-4 is where it's at

There's your cliff. At 5e-4 the training clearly gets unstable, 62.0 compared with 74.2 at 1e-4. With run-f and run-g in, your v1 curve is 5e-5 at 73.1, 1e-4 at 74.2, 2e-4 at 71.4, and 5e-4 at 62.0. That's a well-shaped experiment. A natural follow-up would be trying 1.5e-4 or 7e-5, but diminishing returns are probably kicking in.

ok so next I'm gonna do a hash file for the eval set like you said. sha256 of every example, saved in the repo, and the dedup script fails loudly if any training example matches. I wrote it in like 15 min

That's a solid guardrail. One extra suggestion is to normalize before hashing, lowercasing and stripping punctuation and extra whitespace, so near-duplicates with a changed comma or capital letter don't slip through. Also run it as a step that blocks training, rather than something you remember to do.

ooh normalizing, yeah. wtf why didn't I think of that. ok espresso is giving me trouble again, new bag, tried 14 and shots were 25 sec, 18g, 36 out, sour af. went to 12 and 32 sec, 36 out, bitter. ugh. the 13 is in between and was 29 so maybe the grinder just has a huge step between 12 and 14

That's very plausible. Stepped grinders can have jumps that are bigger than the sweet spot is wide. Since 13 gave you around 29 seconds and tasted sweet before, go back to it and fine tune with dose or yield rather than grind. If you want a smaller adjustment, a half step on your dial, 12.5, may help you land between 29 and 32 seconds.
half step it is. sleep news: bo had a rough night, 2:50 wake, but then went back down in like 10 min on his own! first time ever

Going back down on his own after 10 minutes is a real milestone. That's self-soothing, which is the skill that makes sleep regressions pass. Try to stay out of the room for a few minutes on those wakes and give him the chance to do it again. It might take a few more nights to become reliable.
hell yes. ok also my son's daycare teacher said he was super emotional today, cried when his friend took a truck. kids man. so what is the deal with the 2 year thing, is it the terrible twos or what

It's partly that, and partly just developmental. At two, toddlers have big feelings and not many words yet, plus a growing sense of independence. Sleep disruptions, molars, and a big language explosion all tend to overlap, so emotions run high. Naming the feeling, like "you're sad because he took your truck," helps them build the vocabulary to cope.

yeah naming feelings is the thing. we do that. ok one more model thing, I want to eventually do a 1b model that looks stuff up when it doesn't know a word. but thats later. for now I just want the best slang one from these runs

Makes sense. Getting a solid base model first, then adding a lookup tool on top, is a reasonable order. For the base model, what matters is your best clean-eval run, since that's the one you'll build the lookup behavior on.

also unrelated, I keep meaning to ask. is it worth writing all these runs into a spreadsheet or just keep the table in my notes app. I already lost one run's logs when I overwrote a folder and I was so mad at myself

A spreadsheet is worth it, mostly because you can add columns as you learn what matters, like dataset version, eval subset, learning rate, lora rank, and the date. Also keep the raw logs in per-run folders that never get reused. Losing logs is the kind of mistake you only make once, but a naming convention prevents it entirely.
ok spreadsheet. columns for run name, data version, lr, eval set used, score, and a notes column for stuff like "leaked". that'll do it
That covers it. Add the lora rank and epoch count too, and you'll be able to reproduce any row later without digging through old chat or logs.
lol ok yeah. anyway last thing, bo woke up at 5:20 today, and the bedtime is back to 7:15 and its been like 9 days. I think the molar thing is real cause he was drooling all day yesterday

That fits the molar theory, drooling and chewing on everything are classic signs. A 5:20 wake is a big improvement over 3:40, so I'd say the overall trend is positive across those 9 days even with some bad nights. If the molars break through in the next week or two, you may see another improvement. Keep the routine and you'll likely land somewhere good.

**run-c wins: lr 1e-4 on v1 data, scoring 74.2.**

That's the real number. run-c was trained on v1, which had zero overlap with the eval set, and when we rescored it on the 688 clean examples it barely moved (about 0.1), so there's no leak inflating it.

How the clean board shakes out:

| run | data | lr | clean score |
|---|---|---|---|
| **run-c** | v1 | **1e-4** | **74.2** |

If you want to be sure before you build word lookup on top of it, rerun c, f and e with a couple of different seeds and see if the order holds. If it doesn't, you've got a three-way tie, and run-c is still a perfectly good base for Llama 3.2 1B (LoRA r16, alpha 32, 3 epochs, batch 8, same as all the others).

tests.title: Best-man stories
tests.trap: The groom is Moose, and so is a houseplant. The bride vetoed one story.
tests.question: ok so which stories about moose am i actually allowed to use lol
turns: ok so i need help with something and i have literally no idea where to start. my buddy Marcus is getting married in like 5 weeks and i got asked to be best man and i have to give a speech and i am freaking out a little bit. everybody calls him Moose btw, has since freshman year of college, long story, so if i say moose thats him

Congrats on being asked, that's a real honor, and five weeks is plenty of time. Good to know about Marcus going by Moose, I'll use that.

A best-man speech usually works best at 3 to 5 minutes, which is about 400 to 600 words spoken. A reliable structure is: a quick opener that introduces who you are, one or two stories that show who he is, a turn toward the bride, and a toast. To get started, tell me a bit about Moose and about his fiancée, and any stories that come to mind, even messy ones. We can sort out what's usable later.

her name is Priya, shes awesome, way too good for him honestly lol. they met at a climbing gym like 4 years ago. ok stories. idk theres a million. the funniest one is probably the camping trip in like 2017 where moose got his head stuck in a bear proof trash can at the campsite. like fully stuck. he was trying to see if a hot dog had fallen in there or some dumb shit and we had to like grease him out with sunscreen and it took 3 of us and a ranger showed up

That is a great story, and it's the kind of thing a wedding crowd loves because it's embarrassing but harmless. The ranger showing up is a perfect beat. For the speech you'd want to keep it tight: setup (camping, hot dog), the stuck moment, the sunscreen rescue, and then a button line that ties it back to him, something like "that's the guy Priya signed up for, someone who'll stick his head into anything for a good cause."

Do you have any stories on the sweeter side too? The best speeches usually have one laugh story and one that lands in the heart.
yeah ok hold on i gotta think. oh wait actually also i need to do my taxes like this week and ive been avoiding it sooo hard. can we talk about that real quick because its stressing me out

Sure, we can switch. Taxes are a lot easier once you get everything into one pile. What's your situation? Are you a regular W-2 employee, do you have any freelance or side income, and do you know what filing software or method you're planning to use? Also, do you have a deadline in mind, or are you filing late or on extension?

ugh ok so i have a regular job W-2 but i also did some freelance photo editing last year for like 3 clients and i have no idea how that works. and i think i filed an extension?? or maybe i meant to. i dont remember. wtf

That's a common mix. For the freelance income: you report it on Schedule C as self-employed income, and you owe self-employment tax (about 15.3 percent) on your net profit in addition to regular income tax. The good news is you can deduct business expenses, like editing software subscriptions, a portion of your computer cost, and so on.

On the extension: check your IRS online account or look for a confirmation email from whatever software you used. If you filed Form 4868, the extension gives you more time to file, not more time to pay, so if you owed anything it would have started accruing interest. If you can't find proof, the safest move is to just file as soon as you can.

ok that makes me feel slightly less dead. i think i did file it, theres an email somewhere. anyway also my plants are dying and i feel like thats related to my life falling apart lol. i have like 6 plants. one is a monstera that i named Moose cuz it was huge and goofy looking when i got it and honestly it looks kinda like it got its head stuck in something too

Ha, the plant Moose. I'll keep the two Mooses straight: Moose the monstera and Moose the groom. Though if the plant also has a head-stuck vibe, there might be a joke in there.

What's going wrong with the plants? Yellowing leaves, brown tips, drooping? Tell me about the light they get and how often you water, and I can narrow it down.

so the monstera has yellow leaves, like 3 of them. and a pothos thats kinda leggy and sad. a snake plant that i think is fine??? and a fiddle leaf fig that is dropping leaves like its going out of style. and 2 little succulents that are kinda squishy

Squishy succulents and yellow monstera leaves both point to overwatering as the most common culprit, so that's my first suspect. Here's a quick read on each:

Monstera: a few yellow leaves is often overwatering or the plant shedding old lower leaves. Check that the top inch or two of soil is dry before watering again. Pothos: leggy means it wants more light, so move it closer to a window and trim the long vines, which you can root in water. Snake plant: if it looks fine, leave it alone, they thrive on neglect. Fiddle leaf fig: these are dramatic, and leaf drop usually comes from a change in light or temperature, or inconsistent watering. Succulents: squishy usually means rot, so stop watering and check the roots.

How often are you watering, and is it on a schedule?
i water everything every sunday lol like a robot. same amount for all of them. thats bad isnt it

Yes, that's likely the root of most of this. A fixed schedule is easy to remember but plants don't all drink at the same rate. Succulents and snake plants might need water every two to four weeks, while a monstera is happy with a drink about once a week in summer and less in winter.

A simple replacement: every Sunday, do a finger test. Push a finger into the soil about two inches. If it's damp, skip. If it's dry, water thoroughly until it drains out the bottom. Takes 30 seconds per plant and saves most of them.

The catch is the "exclusive" part. If your desk is the same one you use for your W-2 job and you also edit photos there, it's tricky. If you have a dedicated corner used only for freelance editing, you might qualify. The simplified method gives you $5 per square foot up to 300 square feet.

That's fine, and the software is legitimately deductible if you use it for the freelance work. If you also use Adobe for personal stuff, you should deduct only the business-use portion. Yes, that could well be your fiddle leaf fig's problem. They hate drafts, especially cold or hot air blowing on them from a vent, and that can cause leaf drop. Correct. Most free versions only cover simple returns, and Schedule C for self-employment income typically requires a paid tier. If the bottom is mush, the stem has rotted. Take the plant out of the pot, cut away any black or mushy parts with clean scissors, and let the healthy part dry out for a few days so the cut end callouses over. Then replant in dry, gritty cactus mix, and wait about a week before watering lightly. If a leaf is still plump, you can even try propagating it by letting it callous and placing it on top of soil.

Seven weeks is tight but doable. Start by nailing down your hard numbers: max monthly rent, the neighborhoods you'd actually live in, and your move-in window. Good, a firm cap makes this much easier. A common rule is rent under about a third of gross income, and you also want to account for utilities, parking, and any pet or amenity fees, which can quietly add a couple hundred a month. my girlfriends family is from guadalajara so i wanna not be a total mute at thanksgiving or whatever. her abuela doesnt speak much english and i just stand there smiling like a golden retriever

The classic move is to disable the last mod you added and see if it launches. If it does, that mod is the culprit or conflicts with something else. If it still crashes, run the load order through LOOT to sort it, and check for missing masters, which are the plugins a mod depends on. Do you get a crash log, or does it just close?
it just closes. no error. SKSE is installed tho

With SKSE you can get more useful logs. Look in Documents/My Games/Skyrim Special Edition/SKSE for a log like skse64.log, and if you have Crash Logger or the like installed, check its output. Nope, for a first mod you can reuse an existing mesh. Duplicate the iron sword, rename it, tweak the damage and weight, and you've got a new item. You only need 3D modeling if you want a totally new look, and that's a much bigger learning curve with Blender and Nifskope.

Yes, the Creation Kit is notorious for crashing, especially when you do a lot of things quickly. Save often, make backups of your plugin file, and install the CK Fixes mod, which patches a bunch of its worst stability bugs. Don't edit your plugin while the game is running, either.

ok switching gears again lol spanish. do you know any good phrases for meeting someones mom. her mom is gonna be at thanksgiving too, and she's kinda scary

Here are some solid ones: "Mucho gusto, señora" (nice to meet you), "Es un placer conocerla" (a pleasure to meet you, formal), "Gracias por recibirme en su casa" (thanks for having me in your home), and "¿Puedo ayudarle con algo?" usted vs tu thing confuses me. when do i use which

"Tú" is informal, for friends, peers, kids, and family you're close to. "Usted" is formal, for elders, strangers, and people you want to show respect to. In Mexico, many people use usted with older relatives and in-laws, so with your girlfriend's mom and abuela, start with usted until they invite you to use tú. If they say "tutéame," that's an invitation to switch.
ok "tuteame" lol. got it. oh also, small thing, can i get a good game to play while i learn? like in spanish

Spanish generally uses a definite article where English wouldn't, especially when talking about things in general. "La pizza" means pizza as a category, "me gusta la música" literally uses "the music," and "el café" works the same way. So when you say your favorite food is pizza, Spanish treats "pizza" as a general noun and wants "la." There are exceptions, but a decent rule is that in Spanish a general noun as the subject or after "es" in this kind of sentence usually gets an article. It will feel natural after enough repetition, and Duolingo is great at drilling this specifically.

Lots of buildings are replacing carpet anyway. If they say yes, get it written into the lease. If they say yes, Riverside basically wins.
2. **Ask if the $200 hold is refundable, in writing.** If it is, pay it. That locks the unit and takes the Friday pressure off.
3. **Go to the Maple showing tomorrow anyway.** It's hardwood throughout and $1700 with parking, and it has no carpet issue. The tradeoff is a tiny kitchen and no dishwasher. Even if you still pick Riverside, you'll know it was a real choice and not just being worn out.
4. While you've got them on the phone, ask about blinds and average electric bills, since those windows face south.

If they won't touch the carpet, you have two options. You can decide on purpose that the kitchen is worth breaking your own dealbreaker, knowing you might need a good air purifier and might regret it. Or you can take Maple and make the rolling cart work. Either is fine as long as you choose it on purpose, not because you're tired of looking.

Want me to write up a quick text to send the Riverside landlord today asking about the carpet and the hold?

tests.question: Going back to the director of that shark movie from the start, what else notable happened on the exact day he was born, and why was that day important?
turns: I'm in the mood for a casual trivia session. Let's start easy. Who directed Jaws?

Jaws was directed by Steven Spielberg. It was released in 1975, when he was still in his twenties, and it is widely credited as the first modern summer blockbuster. The production was famously troubled, since the mechanical shark kept malfunctioning, which forced Spielberg to suggest the shark through music and camera work instead of showing it. That restraint arguably made the film scarier.
Nice. Next one: what is Emma Stone's real name?

Emma Stone's birth name is Emily Jean Stone. She began going by Emma professionally because the Screen Actors Guild already had a member named Emily Stone, and union rules do not allow two members to share the same professional name. She has since won two Academy Awards, one for La La Land and one for Poor Things.
Okay, some math. What is 79,500 times 2?
79,500 times 2 is 159,000. You can check it by doubling 79,000 to get 158,000 and doubling 500 to get 1,000, then adding the two results together.
What is the capital of Australia?

The capital of Australia is Canberra. Many people guess Sydney or Melbourne, because those are the largest cities, but Canberra was purpose-built as the capital in the early twentieth century as a compromise between the two rivals. It sits in the Australian Capital Territory, roughly between Sydney and Melbourne.
What is the chemical symbol for gold?

The chemical symbol for gold is Au. It comes from the Latin word for gold, aurum, which means shining dawn. Gold has atomic number 79, and it is one of the few metals that is naturally found in a relatively pure, uncombined form.
Which planet in our solar system is the largest?

Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system. It is a gas giant with a mass of more than twice that of all the other planets combined. Its Great Red Spot is a storm that has been observed for well over a century, and it is larger than the entire Earth, although it has been shrinking in recent decades.

The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci, who worked on it in the early sixteenth century. It hangs in the Louvre Museum in Paris, where it is protected behind bulletproof glass. The sitter is generally believed to be Lisa Gherardini, the wife of a Florentine silk merchant named Francesco del Giocondo.
How many bones are in the adult human body?

An adult human body has 206 bones. Babies are born with significantly more, often cited as around 270 to 300, because many of their bones are made partly of cartilage and gradually fuse together as they grow. The smallest bone is the stapes in the middle ear, and the largest is the femur in the thigh.
In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?

The Berlin Wall fell in 1989. The border crossings were opened on the night of November 9, after a confusing announcement by an East German official. Crowds gathered at the checkpoints, and soon people began climbing on and chipping away at the wall. Germany was formally reunified the following year, on October 3, 1990.
What is the currency of Japan?

The currency of Japan is the yen. Its symbol is ¥ and its international code is JPY. The yen was introduced in 1871 during the Meiji era, and it is one of the most heavily traded currencies in the world, often treated as a safe haven during periods of financial uncertainty.

Pride and Prejudice was written by Jane Austen and published in 1813. It follows Elizabeth Bennet and her complicated relationship with the wealthy and proud Mr. Darcy. Austen published it anonymously, with the title page crediting only the author of Sense and Sensibility, her earlier novel.
What is the square root of 144?
The square root of 144 is 12, since 12 times 12 equals 144. It is also a handy number because 144 is a dozen dozen, which has traditionally been called a gross.
Now go back to that director I asked about at the start. Who did the guy who directed Jaws marry?

Steven Spielberg has been married twice. His first wife was the actress Amy Irving, whom he married in 1985. They had a son, Max, and divorced in 1989. In 1991 he married the actress Kate Capshaw, whom he had met when she was cast in Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, which he directed. They remain married and have a blended family with several children.

Steven Spielberg was born on December 18, 1946, in Cincinnati, Ohio. His family later moved to New Jersey, then Arizona, and then to California, where he made amateur films as a teenager and eventually broke into television and then feature films.
Thanks. Let's change gears. What is the tallest mountain above sea level?

Mount Everest is the tallest mountain above sea level. Its official height is 8,849 meters, or about 29,032 feet, according to the measurement agreed upon by Nepal and China in 2020. It sits on the border between Nepal and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China in the Himalayas.
Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?

Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon. He stepped onto the surface on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission, and Buzz Aldrin followed him shortly afterward. Michael Collins stayed in lunar orbit aboard the command module. Armstrong's famous line was "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."
Fifteen percent of 240 is 36. One easy way to do this is to take 10 percent, which is 24, then add half of that, which is 12, giving you 36.
What is the hardest naturally occurring substance?

Diamond is generally considered the hardest naturally occurring substance, rating 10 on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness. It is made entirely of carbon atoms arranged in a rigid crystal structure. Despite being so hard, a diamond can still be shattered by a sharp blow in the right direction, because hardness is different from toughness.
What is the fastest land animal?

The cheetah is the fastest land animal. It can reach speeds of roughly 100 to 120 kilometers per hour, or about 60 to 75 miles per hour, in short bursts that usually last less than a minute. Its long legs, flexible spine, and semi-retractable claws help it accelerate faster than most sports cars.

George Orwell wrote 1984, which was published in 1949. Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair. The novel introduced concepts such as Big Brother, doublethink, and thoughtcrime, which have since become common shorthand for discussing surveillance and authoritarian control.
What is the capital of Canada?

The capital of Canada is Ottawa, which is located in the province of Ontario, right on the border with Quebec. Like Canberra, it is not the country's largest city. That title belongs to Toronto. Queen Victoria chose Ottawa as the capital in 1857.
Which composer wrote the Ninth Symphony that includes the Ode to Joy?

That was Ludwig van Beethoven. His Ninth Symphony premiered in Vienna in 1824, and by then he was almost completely deaf. The final movement sets a poem by Friedrich Schiller to music for a choir and soloists, and it was the first time a major composer included human voices in a symphony. The Ode to Joy melody is also the official anthem of the European Union.
What year did the Titanic sink?

The Titanic sank in 1912. It struck an iceberg late on the night of April 14 and went down in the early hours of April 15 in the North Atlantic, on its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York. More than 1,500 of the roughly 2,200 people aboard died.

Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 at St. Mary's Hospital in London. He noticed that a mold called Penicillium had contaminated one of his bacterial culture dishes and that the bacteria near the mold had been killed. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain later developed it into a usable drug, and the three men shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
How many strings does a standard violin have?

A standard violin has four strings, tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A, and E, from lowest to highest. The same tuning pattern is used for the viola, though it is pitched lower, and the cello, which is pitched lower still.
Which planet is known as the Red Planet?

Mars is known as the Red Planet. Its color comes from iron oxide, essentially rust, on its surface and in its dust. Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, which stands about two and a half times as high as Mount Everest.

Hamlet was written by William Shakespeare, probably around 1600 or 1601. It is his longest play, and it tells the story of the Prince of Denmark, who seeks revenge against his uncle Claudius for murdering his father. The line "To be, or not to be" comes from this play.
What is the largest ocean on Earth?

The Pacific Ocean is the largest, covering about a third of the planet's surface. It is larger than all of the Earth's land area combined. It also contains the deepest known point in the world's oceans, the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, which reaches roughly 11,000 meters below the surface.
What is the boiling point of water at sea level in Fahrenheit?

Water boils at 212 degrees Fahrenheit at standard sea-level pressure, which is 100 degrees Celsius. At higher altitudes the air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature, which is why cooking times can be longer in the mountains.
Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?

Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. She received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with her husband Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, for their work on radioactivity. In 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for discovering polonium and radium, which made her the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
What is the longest river in the world?

The Nile is traditionally cited as the longest river in the world at roughly 6,650 kilometers, or about 4,130 miles, flowing north through northeastern Africa into the Mediterranean Sea. Some measurements argue that the Amazon is longer, depending on where its source is defined, so there is a small amount of debate, but the Nile is the answer most references give.
What is the smallest prime number?

The smallest prime number is 2. It is also the only even prime number, because every other even number is divisible by 2 and therefore has at least three divisors. The next primes are 3, 5, 7, and 11.
Which country has the most time zones, counting its overseas territories?

France has the most time zones when overseas territories are counted, with 12 in total, or 13 if you include its claim in Antarctica. This is because it still governs places such as French Polynesia, French Guiana, Réunion, and New Caledonia, spread across the globe.
Last one for now. What is the approximate speed of light in a vacuum?

The speed of light in a vacuum is about 299,792 kilometers per second, which is roughly 186,000 miles per second. It is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second by definition, since the meter is now defined in terms of the distance light travels in a tiny fraction of a second.
Okay, a few more. What is the largest desert in the world?

The largest desert in the world is Antarctica, if you define a desert by low precipitation rather than heat. It receives very little precipitation each year, and it covers about 14 million square kilometers. The largest hot desert is the Sahara in northern Africa, which spans roughly 9 million square kilometers, about the size of the United States.
How many players are on the field for one soccer team during a match?

Each soccer team has eleven players on the field at once, including the goalkeeper. A team is usually allowed to name a number of substitutes, and in most professional competitions up to five substitutions are now permitted during a match, though the exact rules depend on the competition. A match lasts ninety minutes, divided into two halves of forty-five minutes, plus stoppage time.
Who developed the theory of general relativity?

Albert Einstein developed the theory of general relativity, which he completed and presented in November 1915. It describes gravity not as a force pulling objects together but as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. The theory was dramatically supported in 1919, when observations during a solar eclipse showed that starlight bent around the Sun by roughly the amount he had predicted.

Twelve times twelve times twelve is 1,728. You get there by multiplying 12 by 12 to get 144, then multiplying 144 by 12, which is 1,440 plus 288, giving 1,728. That number is also the number of cubic inches in a cubic foot.
What is the main language spoken in Brazil?

The main language spoken in Brazil is Portuguese. It is the only country in South America where Portuguese is the official language, a legacy of Portuguese colonization beginning in the early sixteenth century. Most of its neighbors speak Spanish. Brazilian Portuguese differs from the European variety in pronunciation, vocabulary, and some grammar.
What gas do plants absorb from the atmosphere for photosynthesis?

Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Using energy from sunlight, they combine it with water to produce glucose, a sugar they use for energy and growth, and they release oxygen as a byproduct. This process takes place mainly in the leaves, in structures called chloroplasts that contain the green pigment chlorophyll.
Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?

Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. The choice honored ancient Greece, the birthplace of the original Olympics. The Games were revived largely through the efforts of the French educator Pierre de Coubertin, and around 240 athletes from about a dozen countries took part, all of them men. The marathon was introduced at these Games, and it was won by the Greek runner Spyridon Louis.

By the most common convention taught in English-speaking countries, there are seven continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (sometimes called Oceania), Europe, North America, and South America. Other countries teach slightly different models, for example combining North and South America into a single continent, or treating Europe and Asia as one landmass called Eurasia.
What is the freezing point of water in Celsius?

Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, which is 32 degrees Fahrenheit, at standard atmospheric pressure. The Celsius scale was originally defined using the freezing and boiling points of water, with 100 degrees between them, which is why those two values are so convenient to remember.

Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889. He created it while staying at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in southern France, and the view in the painting is based on the scene from his bedroom window, though the village was partly invented. It now hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
And what is the capital of Italy?

The capital of Italy is Rome. It has been a major city for more than two thousand years, and it was the center of the Roman Republic and later the Roman Empire. The Vatican City, the smallest independent state in the world, is an enclave entirely inside the city.
What is the chemical formula for table salt?

The chemical formula for table salt is NaCl, which stands for sodium chloride. It is made up of sodium and chlorine in a one-to-one ratio, held together in a crystal lattice by ionic bonds. Both of its elements are dangerous on their own, since sodium reacts violently with water and chlorine is a toxic gas, but combined they form a compound essential to life.
How many sides does a hexagon have?

A hexagon has six sides. The interior angles of any simple hexagon add up to 720 degrees, and in a regular hexagon each angle measures 120 degrees. Honeycombs are made of hexagonal cells because the shape tiles a flat surface with no gaps while using the least amount of wax.
