tests.title: Japan trip
tests.trap: Dates, sister, wheelchair, budget and a temple, all stated plainly early on.
tests.question: Can you put together a day-by-day plan for the trip we talked about?
turns: Hello. I would like some help planning a trip to Japan. Do you have time to talk it through with me?

Absolutely, I would be glad to help. Japan is a wonderful destination, and a little planning goes a long way. To start, could you tell me when you hope to travel, how long you plan to stay, and who will be going with you?
Certainly. I plan to travel from April 12 to April 16, 2027, which is five days in total. I will be going with my sister, Maya.

That is a great window. Mid-April is just after the peak cherry blossom season in most of central Japan, so you may still see some late blossoms, especially in higher-elevation areas, and the weather is usually mild. Five days is short, so it helps to choose a small number of places rather than trying to cover the whole country. Do you have a rough budget in mind?
Yes. Our budget is 250 US dollars per day for the two of us combined. That should cover food, local transportation, and admission fees. Flights are being handled separately.

Thank you, that is helpful. Two hundred fifty dollars a day for two people is workable in Japan if you are thoughtful. Meals can be very affordable, and many temples charge only a few hundred yen for entry. I will keep that figure in mind as we go. Is there anything in particular you are hoping to see?
There is one place I really want to visit. It is Kiyomizu-dera, the temple in Kyoto. I have wanted to see it for many years.

Kiyomizu-dera is a lovely choice. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, famous for its large wooden stage that juts out from the hillside and offers views over the city. It sits on a hill in eastern Kyoto, so the approach involves some slopes and steps, which is worth planning around. Is there anything about your travel needs that I should know?
Yes, that is important. My sister uses a wheelchair, so accessibility will matter for almost everything we do.

Thank you for telling me. I will make sure the suggestions we discuss take that into account, including step-free train stations, accessible hotel rooms, and routes that avoid long staircases. Japan has made real progress on accessibility, though older sites like temples can still be challenging. We can look at that in detail when we get to the Kiyomizu-dera visit.
That sounds good. Before we go further, may I switch to a different subject for a little while? I need help with something from work.
Of course. Planning trips is easier when you can step away and come back. What do you need help with?
I have to write an email to my team about moving our weekly meeting from Tuesday to Thursday. Some people have a conflict on Tuesdays. I would like it to be friendly but clear.

Here is a draft you can adjust.

Subject: Weekly meeting moving to Thursdays

Hello everyone,

Starting next week, our weekly team meeting will move from Tuesday to Thursday at the same time. A few of you have standing conflicts on Tuesdays, and Thursday appears to work for everyone.

I will send an updated calendar invitation today. If Thursday creates a problem for you, please let me know by the end of this week so we can find a solution.

Thank you for your flexibility.

Best regards,
[Your name]
That is very good. Could you make it slightly shorter and add a line asking people to update their calendars?

Certainly. Here is a shorter version.

Subject: Weekly meeting moving to Thursdays

Hello everyone,

Beginning next week, our weekly meeting will move from Tuesday to Thursday at the same time. Please update your calendars accordingly. If Thursday is a problem for you, let me know by Friday.

Thank you,
[Your name]

Perfect, thank you. I will send that this afternoon. Now I have a question about something completely different. I have a pothos plant at home, and a few of the leaves are turning yellow. What might be wrong?

Yellow leaves on a pothos are most often caused by overwatering. Roots that sit in soggy soil cannot get enough oxygen, and the leaves respond by yellowing. Other causes include too little light, a pot without drainage holes, or a sudden change in environment. Check whether the soil is wet several inches down, and whether the pot drains freely.
The soil does feel quite damp, and I have been watering once a week. The pot does have drainage holes.

Then I would cut back. Pothos prefer to dry out partway between waterings. Try letting the top two inches of soil become dry before you water again, which may mean every ten days or two weeks, depending on your home. Remove the yellow leaves, since they will not recover, and empty any water that collects in the saucer. New growth should look healthy within a few weeks.
That is helpful. Should it be in direct sunlight?

No, pothos do best in bright, indirect light. Direct sun can scorch the leaves, while very dim corners can slow growth and make the vines leggy. A spot a few feet from a window, or near a window with a sheer curtain, is ideal. They are quite forgiving, so you do not need to be exact.
Wonderful. I will move it closer to the window but away from direct sun. Now, going back to the trip for a moment. Where do you think we should stay, given that I want to see Kiyomizu-dera?

Since Kiyomizu-dera is in Kyoto, basing yourselves in Kyoto for most of the trip makes sense. Staying near Kyoto Station is often the best choice for a wheelchair user, because the station has elevators and wide gates, and it connects to the bullet train, the airport express, and local lines. Many hotels there offer accessible rooms with roll-in or wide-entry bathrooms. Would you prefer a single base for all five nights?
Yes, I think one base would be easier for Maya. We would arrive on April 12 and leave on April 16, so that would be four nights.

That is right, four nights from April 12 to April 16. Staying in one place reduces the number of times you need to move luggage and a wheelchair, which is a real benefit. Arriving at Kansai International Airport and taking the Haruka express to Kyoto Station is a straightforward option, and the Haruka has space for wheelchairs if you reserve in advance. Do you know which airport you will fly into?
We will fly into Kansai International Airport, so that works well. How much should we expect to spend on an accessible hotel room? I want to stay within our budget.

Because your daily budget of 250 dollars covers food, transport, and admissions, I would treat the hotel as a separate matter unless you tell me otherwise. Is the hotel included in the 250 dollars, or is it separate?
Good question. The hotel is separate. We have already set aside money for lodging, so the 250 dollars per day is only for food, transportation, and admissions.

Thank you for clarifying. That gives you a comfortable amount to work with. Two people can eat well for around 80 to 100 dollars a day, local transport is modest, and admissions are small, so you will likely have room for a special meal or a guided experience. I will plan within the 250 dollars per day.
That is good to hear. Let me ask about something else. Could you recommend a book? I enjoy novels that are thoughtful but not too long.

I would be happy to. A few suggestions: "Klara and the Sun" by Kazuo Ishiguro is a quiet, moving novel about an artificial friend observing a family. "A Gentleman in Moscow" by Amor Towles is longer, but very warm and engaging. If you would like something shorter, "The Remains of the Day" by Ishiguro is a classic of restraint and regret. Which sounds closest to your taste?
I have read Ishiguro before and liked him. Is there something related to Japan, since I am going there soon?

Yes. "Convenience Store Woman" by Sayaka Murata is short, funny, and strange, and offers a distinctive view of modern Japanese life. "The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle" by Haruki Murakami is a much longer, dreamlike novel. For something gentler, "Strange Weather in Tokyo" by Hiromi Kawakami is a quiet love story told through shared meals. I would suggest Convenience Store Woman as a quick read before your trip.
I like the sound of Convenience Store Woman. I will look for a copy this weekend. Thank you.
You are welcome. It is only about 160 pages, so you could finish it in an evening or two. Would you like to return to the trip planning now, or is there something else on your mind?
Let us return to the trip. Can you tell me about getting around Kyoto with a wheelchair?

Certainly. Kyoto's subway has elevators at every station, and the two lines, the Karasuma and the Tozai, are generally accessible. City buses are the main way to reach many temples, and most newer buses have low floors and a ramp that the driver deploys. Drivers are usually helpful, though buses can be crowded at peak times. Accessible taxis, sometimes called universal design taxis, can be booked and are a good option for hillier destinations. Many visitors also use regular taxis, which cost more but are very convenient.
How do we pay for the buses and trains? Is there a simple way?

The simplest way is a rechargeable IC card such as ICOCA, Suica, or PASMO. You tap it on entry and exit, and it works on trains, subways, and buses throughout most of Japan. Many travelers now add a Suica or ICOCA card to a mobile wallet on their phone. Neither of you needs to buy individual tickets, which saves time and avoids confusion.
That is very convenient. Let me ask something unrelated first. How do I politely decline an invitation to a coworker's party? I do not want to seem rude.

A short, warm reply works best. For example: "Thank you so much for inviting me. Unfortunately I won't be able to make it, but I hope you have a wonderful time. I would love to hear how it goes." You do not need to give a detailed reason, and keeping it brief usually comes across as gracious rather than rude.
That is exactly the tone I wanted. Thank you. Now, back to Kiyomizu-dera. How accessible is it for a wheelchair user?

It is partly accessible, and it takes some planning. The approach is the main challenge. The streets leading up from Higashiyama, such as Chawan-zaka and Matsubara-dori, are steep and cobbled. A good strategy is to take a taxi, preferably an accessible one, directly to the temple area, and enter by the quieter approach where the ground is gentler. Inside the grounds, the main hall and the famous stage have steps in places, and some areas have ramps or a designated accessible route. The temple has historically offered a slope route for visitors who cannot use stairs, and staff are generally willing to help. It is wise to check the temple's current accessibility information before you go.
That is very useful. What time of day is best to visit so we avoid crowds?

Early morning is best. Kiyomizu-dera typically opens around 6:00 in the morning, long before the tour groups arrive, and the light on the wooden stage is beautiful. Arriving between 6:00 and 8:00 gives you space to move at Maya's pace without being jostled. Late afternoon is the second-best option, and the temple sometimes holds special evening openings in spring, so it is worth checking whether one coincides with your dates.
An early start sounds good. Do you know the entrance fee?

The general admission fee has been around 500 yen per person, which is roughly three to four dollars. Wheelchair users and their companions may qualify for a reduced rate or free entry at many Japanese sites, so it is worth asking at the ticket booth. Either way, the cost is very small compared with your daily budget.
Excellent. Another quick question about work. How can I ask my manager for a day off on April 12 without sounding demanding?

Frame it as a request with a plan. For example: "I would like to request vacation from April 12 through April 16. I will make sure my current projects are covered, and I am happy to prepare handoff notes beforehand. Please let me know if this works." Asking well in advance and offering to arrange coverage shows consideration. It is also wise to send the request in writing so there is a record.
Thank you. I will send something like that tomorrow. Back to the trip: what else should we see besides Kiyomizu-dera, given that we only have a few days?

Here are a few suggestions that suit a wheelchair and a modest pace. Nijo Castle has wide paths and a clear route, though the interior has some steps. The Kyoto Imperial Palace Park is flat and spacious. Fushimi Inari's famous torii gates involve many stairs, but the lower section near the entrance is manageable, and you can enjoy the atmosphere without climbing. Arashiyama's bamboo grove has a mostly flat main path, and the riverside area is pleasant. The Nishiki Market is lively, though narrow and crowded, so a weekday morning is better.
Those all sound good. Maya especially likes gardens. Are there any good gardens that are wheelchair friendly?

Yes. The Kyoto Botanical Garden has broad, flat paths and a large greenhouse, and it is easy to reach by subway. The Shosei-en garden near Kyoto Station is small, quiet, and close to your hotel area, which makes it a good low-effort stop. Heian Shrine's garden is also lovely in spring, though some paths are gravel, which is harder for wheels. I would prioritize the botanical garden and Shosei-en.
Wonderful. How much would a day of meals cost for us?

You can eat very well for little. A good lunch at a casual restaurant is about 1,000 to 1,500 yen per person, and dinner at a small restaurant is often 2,000 to 3,500 yen per person. Convenience stores, called konbini, also sell surprisingly good food for breakfast. A typical day of meals for two comes to roughly 60 to 100 dollars, so you will stay comfortably within your 250 dollar daily budget with room for transport and admissions.
That is reassuring. Let me ask a different question. What is a good way to remember to water my plants regularly?

A recurring calendar reminder works well. Set one for every week as a prompt to check the soil rather than to water automatically, since the right schedule depends on dryness. Some people also attach the habit to something they already do, such as checking the plants every Sunday morning with their coffee. A small sticky note near the plant can also help.
I like the idea of checking the soil rather than watering by schedule. I will set the reminder. Now, back to Japan once more. Will we need a visa?

That depends on your passport. Citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and many other countries can enter Japan for up to 90 days for tourism without a visa. You will need a passport that is valid for the length of your stay. Please check the Japanese embassy's website for your nationality to be sure, because rules can change.
We both hold US passports, so I think we are fine. What about money? Should we carry cash?

Carry some cash. Japan has become much more card friendly, but many small restaurants, temples, and shops still prefer cash. Withdrawing yen at convenience store ATMs, especially those at 7-Eleven, is easy and usually works with foreign cards. I would suggest having around 20,000 to 30,000 yen on hand each day or two, and using a card for larger purchases.
Good to know. Is there anything I should know about taking a wheelchair on the Shinkansen? We might take a day trip.

Wheelchair spaces are available on the Shinkansen, but you must reserve them. On the Tokaido Shinkansen, the wheelchair seating areas are typically located in specific cars, and you can book at a station ticket office, called Midori no Madoguchi, ideally a day or more in advance. Station staff will bring a ramp to the train and assist with boarding and exiting. A day trip to Nara or Osaka does not require the Shinkansen, however, since regular trains are easy and affordable.
Nara sounds appealing. Is it accessible?

Nara Park is largely flat, and the famous deer roam freely, which many visitors love. Todai-ji, with its giant bronze Buddha, has a main hall that is reasonably accessible, with a ramp and level approach in many areas. The trip from Kyoto takes around 45 minutes by the Kintetsu line or about an hour by the JR Nara line. Both have elevators at the main stations. It would make an excellent half-day or full-day outing.
Great, I will consider it. Let me ask for one more recommendation about books. Do you have a suggestion for a nonfiction book about travel?

"The Songs of Trees" is more nature than travel, but a classic of travel writing is "The Road to Oxiana" by Robert Byron, and a more recent favorite is "Vagabonding" by Rolf Potts, which is about the philosophy of slow travel. For Japan specifically, "The Roads to Sata" by Alan Booth describes a long walk across the country and is both funny and tender.
The Roads to Sata sounds interesting. I will add it to my list. Thank you.
You are welcome. It pairs nicely with a first visit to Japan, and it is easier to read in short stretches. Shall we go back to the trip and talk about the daily rhythm of your days?
Yes, please. In general, Maya tires easily, so I would like to avoid packing too much into each day.

That is sensible. A good pattern is one major sight in the morning, a long lunch, a rest at the hotel in the early afternoon, and a lighter activity in the evening. Planning around two main activities per day will feel relaxed and still let you see a lot. Since Maya uses a wheelchair and tires easily, I would also build in plenty of breaks and choose places with benches and accessible restrooms.
That sounds just right. Can you remind me what the dates are, so I can double check my flight booking?
Yes. You told me you will travel from April 12 to April 16, 2027, which is five days in total, with four nights in Kyoto, flying into Kansai International Airport with your sister, Maya.
That matches what I booked. Thank you. One last thing for now. Could you suggest a short thank-you note for my coworker who helped me with a project?

Certainly. Here is a short note.

Hello [Name],

Thank you so much for your help with the project. Your time and careful work made a real difference, and I truly appreciated it. Please let me know if I can return the favor at any point.

With thanks,
[Your name]
That is lovely. Let me ask a practical question about the flight. Is it better to arrange wheelchair assistance with the airline in advance?

Yes, I would strongly recommend it. Contact the airline at least 48 hours before departure, and ideally when you book, to request wheelchair assistance and to note whether Maya can walk short distances or needs help with every transfer. Tell them whether her wheelchair is manual or electric, because a battery-powered chair has specific rules about transport. Airline staff will usually take her to the gate and to the aircraft door, and an aisle chair is used to reach the seat. At Kansai International Airport, staff meet passengers at the arrival gate and help with immigration and baggage claim, which makes the first hour much smoother.
Her wheelchair is a manual folding one. Does that make anything easier?

It does. A manual folding chair is simple to handle on trains, in taxis, and on buses, and it fits in the trunk of most standard taxis once folded. It also avoids battery restrictions on the flight. I would still bring a lightweight cushion and a small repair kit with a tire pump, since cobblestone paths around Kyoto temples can be rough on the wheels. A portable folding ramp is not necessary, as stations and buses provide their own.
That is good advice. Now, switching topics, I need to write a short bio for a company newsletter. I work as a project coordinator and I enjoy hiking and baking. Could you draft three sentences?

Here is a draft.

"[Your name] joined the team as a project coordinator and keeps our schedules and deadlines running smoothly. Outside of work, [he/she/they] enjoy hiking local trails and baking bread on the weekends. Colleagues are encouraged to ask about the sourdough, which has become something of a legend on the third floor."

You can swap in your own details, or I can make the tone more formal if you prefer.
That is charming, but I will keep the tone a little more formal. Could you remove the sourdough sentence?

Certainly.

"[Your name] joined the team as a project coordinator and is responsible for keeping our schedules and deadlines on track. Outside of work, [he/she/they] enjoy hiking local trails and baking at home. [He/She/They] look forward to working with everyone across the organization."

That reads as friendly and professional, and it is easy to trim further if the newsletter has a word limit.
Thank you, that works. Let me return to the trip. Which part of Kyoto should we choose for the hotel, given the budget and Maya's needs?

For your needs I would suggest the area around Kyoto Station or the Karasuma-Oike and Shijo districts in the city center. Kyoto Station offers the best access to the airport express, the Nara line, and the subway, and many hotels there have accessible rooms and elevators from the station directly. The Shijo area is closer to restaurants, Nishiki Market, and the Gion district, and several buses to Kiyomizu-dera run from there. Because your hotel budget is separate, you can choose based on comfort. Please confirm that the room has a wide doorway and a bathroom that Maya can use, and email the hotel directly to ask about step-free access and the bed height.
I will contact the hotel about those details. Should I book the accessible taxi for the Kiyomizu-dera morning?

That is a good idea. Universal design taxis and accessible taxi services in Kyoto can be reserved by phone or through the hotel's front desk, and the hotel staff can usually make the call in Japanese on your behalf. Reserve it a day or two in advance for an early morning pickup around 6:30, since drivers may be limited at that hour. A taxi ride from Kyoto Station to the Kiyomizu-dera area costs roughly 2,000 to 2,500 yen, which is comfortably within your 250 dollar daily budget. Ask the driver to drop you at the entrance nearest the temple gate to minimize the uphill portion.
Wonderful. Do you think we should also see Fushimi Inari, even if we cannot climb?

Yes, I think it is worth a short visit. The shrine is free to enter and open all hours. The main shrine buildings and the first stretch of the torii gates near the base are on fairly level ground, and the first few gates offer the photographs most visitors want. Going in the early evening is pleasant, and the train from Kyoto Station on the JR Nara line takes only about five minutes, with an elevator at the station. You do not need to climb the mountain to enjoy it.
That is a relief. What about a final special dinner on our last night, April 15? Something nice but within the budget.

A nice option is a kaiseki or set-course dinner at a restaurant with Western-style seating or tables, since tatami seating on the floor can be difficult for a wheelchair user. Many places in Kyoto offer lunch versions of kaiseki for roughly 4,000 to 6,000 yen per person, which is cheaper than dinner and very satisfying. Alternatively, a yakitori or tempura counter dinner for around 5,000 yen each would feel like a treat. Please call ahead to confirm there is a step-free entrance and a table that can accommodate a wheelchair.
A lunch kaiseki sounds like a better value. I will consider that for April 15. Let me ask a final unrelated question. Is it a good idea to repot the pothos now, or should I wait?

Repot only if the plant is clearly root-bound, meaning roots are circling the pot or growing out of the drainage holes. Since yours is showing stress from overwatering, I would wait until it recovers. Spring is the best season to repot, so if you see healthy new growth in a few weeks, you could move it into a pot one size larger with fresh, well-draining soil. Repotting a stressed plant can add strain it does not need.
That makes sense. I will wait and watch it. Thank you for all of this. I think that is all for now, and I will come back soon so we can organize everything into a plan.
That sounds good. When you return, we can turn everything we have discussed into a clear day-by-day plan. Enjoy your weekend, and best of luck with the email, the plant, and your new book.

runs.answer:
Here's a day-by-day plan for Kyoto, Apr 12–16, built on the rhythm we settled on: one big thing in the morning, a long lunch, a rest at the hotel, then something light in the evening. Everything assumes one base near Kyoto Station.

**Before you go**
- Email the hotel now and ask them to book an accessible taxi for **Tue Apr 13, ~6:30am** to Kiyomizu-dera. You land the day before, so you can't book it 1–2 days ahead from Kyoto.
- Reserve wheelchair space on the Haruka for both directions.
- Call or email ahead to book the **Thu Apr 15 kaiseki lunch**. Confirm table seating (no tatami) and a step-free entrance.
- Pack: Maya's cushion, the repair kit/pump, and some yen in cash.

**Mon Apr 12 (arrival)**
- KIX → Haruka to Kyoto Station. Pick up ICOCA cards at the airport.
- Check in and rest. Don't plan anything else.
- Evening: an easy dinner in or near Kyoto Station, which is flat with elevators everywhere. Double-check tomorrow's taxi with the front desk.

**Tue Apr 13 (Kiyomizu-dera)**
- 6:30 taxi to the entrance closest to the gate, then the slope route up. Skip Chawan-zaka. Admission is about ¥500; ask whether there's a disability discount.
- Late breakfast or early long lunch nearby, then taxi back.
- Early afternoon: hotel rest. You'll need it after the early start.
- Early evening: **Fushimi Inari, lower gates only.** It's 5 minutes on the JR Nara line, the station has an elevator, and entry is free. Turn back wherever the path starts to climb.

**Wed Apr 14 (garden day for Maya)**
- Morning: **Kyoto Botanical Garden** by subway. It's big and flat with lots of benches. Take it slow.
- Long lunch near the garden or back toward Karasuma.
- Hotel rest.
- Late afternoon: **Shosei-en**, a short trip from the station. It's small and calm, a good gentle second garden. Check its closing time.
- *Nara swap:* If you want the Nara day trip, use this day for it. Kintetsu takes about 45 minutes. Do Nara Park and Todai-ji in the morning, have lunch there, and come back to rest. Move the Botanical Garden to Thursday morning instead of Nishiki.

**Thu Apr 15 (last full day + special lunch)**
- Morning: **Nishiki Market** right around opening, while it's a weekday and still quiet. It's narrow, so go early, before it fills up.
- **Kaiseki lunch** (~¥4,000–6,000 each). Let this be the main event of the day.
- Hotel rest.
- Evening: a slow roll through **Imperial Palace Park**. Or, if Kiyomizu has a spring evening opening that week, go back for the night views.

**Fri Apr 16 (departure)**
- Depending on your flight time: a relaxed breakfast, packing, and maybe a quick final wander around the station area.

Here is a day-by-day plan for April 12 to 16, 2027, with four nights based at Kyoto Station. I have kept it to about two main activities a day for Maya, with rest built in, and I have marked a few optional swaps. April 12 falls on a Monday, so Days 2 to 5 are weekdays.

**Day 1, Monday April 12: Arrival**
- Land at Kansai International Airport and ask for staff assistance at the arrival gate.
- Take the Haruka express to Kyoto Station. Reserve the wheelchair space in advance.
- Check in and rest. Arriving early in the day leaves room for a nap if the travel tires Maya.
- Late afternoon, take a short, easy stroll through Shosei-en, the small garden near the station.
- Have an early dinner at a restaurant with a step-free entrance, close to the hotel.

**Day 2, Tuesday April 13: Kiyomizu-dera**
- Book the accessible taxi a day or two ahead for a 6:30 a.m. pickup, and ask to be dropped at the entrance nearest the temple gate.
- Spend the morning at Kiyomizu-dera while it is quiet. Ask at the ticket booth about any reduced or free rate for Maya and her companion.
- Ask staff about the current accessible route before you go.
- Have lunch in the Higashiyama area, then return to the hotel by midday.
- Rest through the afternoon. In the evening, keep it light, with a short walk near the hotel or the Shijo area if you feel up to it.

**Day 3, Wednesday April 14: Nara day trip**
- Take the JR Nara line from Kyoto Station, which takes about 45 minutes. The Kintetsu line is a similar option.
- Spend the late morning and early afternoon in Nara Park, where the deer roam, and at Todai-ji, which has a level approach and a ramp into the main hall.
- Return to Kyoto by mid-afternoon and rest at the hotel.
- Keep dinner simple and close to the hotel.

**Day 4, Thursday April 15: Gardens, lunch, and Fushimi Inari**
- In the morning, visit the Kyoto Botanical Garden, which has broad, flat paths and a large greenhouse. Take the subway, as you planned earlier.
- Have the lunch kaiseki. Book ahead, and confirm there is a step-free entrance and a table that fits the wheelchair.
- Rest at the hotel in the early afternoon.
- In the early evening, visit the lower section of Fushimi Inari. Take the JR Nara line from Kyoto Station, which is about five minutes, and use the elevator at the station. Stay near the base and the first gates, and skip the climb. If Maya is tired, drop this visit.

**Day 5, Friday April 16: Departure**
- Leave the hotel with a comfortable buffer, and take the Haruka back to Kansai International Airport.
- Request wheelchair assistance with the airline for the return flight as well.
- If your flight leaves late, you could spend an hour at Nishiki Market on a weekday morning, when it is less crowded, or take a short stroll through the flat Kyoto Imperial Palace Park.

**Optional swaps**
- Nijo Castle and the flat main path at Arashiyama's bamboo grove are good options if you want a different day or have extra time.
- If Maya prefers a shorter day, you could swap Nara for Arashiyama. Arashiyama is much closer to the hotel.

**Budget check**
Meals for two should come to roughly $60 to $100 a day, and taxis, the IC card, and admissions add only a modest amount. Each day should stay comfortably inside your $250 daily budget, with room for a special meal.

**Before you go**
- Reserve the Haruka wheelchair seats, the accessible taxi for Day 2, and the kaiseki lunch for Day 4.
- Confirm the hotel room's doorway width and bathroom access, as discussed.
- Load an ICOCA or Suica card onto your phone, and carry some yen for small shops and temples.
- Bring a cushion and a small repair kit with a tire pump for the cobblestones.
- Check opening hours, admission fees, and accessibility details for each site, since these change and I cannot confirm current figures from here.
runs.note: Accurate and accessibility-focused with Kiyomizu-dera taxi and Nara included as a swappable day, though Day 4 stacks garden, kaiseki and Fushimi Inari (softened by the advice to drop Fushimi if Maya is tired).

tests.title: Business arithmetic
tests.trap: Chain two earlier results and a tax amount.
tests.question: Take the monthly revenue number we got earlier, subtract the overall shipping total, and then take off the sales tax amount. What is left?
turns: Hello. I run a small online shop that sells handmade ceramic mugs, and I am trying to organize my numbers in a spreadsheet. Could you help me work through a few calculations in plain language?

Of course. Tell me what you are tracking and which numbers you have, and we can go one calculation at a time. It helps to write each result down in its own cell or labeled row so you can reuse it later. Where would you like to start?
Let us start with revenue. I sell each mug for 24.50 dollars, and last month I sold 1,360 mugs. What was my monthly revenue?

Monthly revenue is the unit price multiplied by the units sold. That is 24.50 × 1,360. Splitting it up: 24 × 1,360 = 32,640, and 0.50 × 1,360 = 680. Added together, that gives 33,320. Your monthly revenue was $33,320.00. In a spreadsheet, if the price is in B1 and the units are in B2, the formula would be =B1*B2.
Great, thank you. Quick unrelated question before I continue. What does the word "ephemeral" mean?

"Ephemeral" describes something that lasts for a very short time. A soap bubble, a morning mist, or a social media story that disappears after a day are all ephemeral. It comes from a Greek word meaning "lasting only a day."
Nice. Now back to the shop. My cost to make each mug is 14.00 dollars. Given my selling price of 24.50, what is my markup percentage?

Markup percentage is the profit per unit divided by the cost per unit. The profit per mug is 24.50 − 14.00 = 10.50. Then 10.50 ÷ 14.00 = 0.75, so your markup is 75 percent. In a spreadsheet, you could use =(B1-B3)/B3, formatted as a percentage, where B3 holds the cost.
Good. Is markup the same thing as profit margin?

No, they are different. Markup is measured against cost, while margin is measured against the selling price. For your mug, the markup is 10.50 ÷ 14.00 = 75 percent. The margin would be 10.50 ÷ 24.50, which is about 42.86 percent. The same dollar profit gives two different percentages because the denominators differ.
That is helpful to know. What is the capital city of Australia?
The capital of Australia is Canberra. Many people guess Sydney or Melbourne, but Canberra was purpose-built as the capital as a compromise between those two rival cities.
Right, I always forget that. Now shipping. Last month I shipped 340 domestic orders, and the average shipping cost was 6.75 dollars per order. What is the total domestic shipping cost?

Multiply the number of orders by the average cost per order: 340 × 6.75. Working it out, 340 × 6 = 2,040 and 340 × 0.75 = 255. Adding them gives 2,295. Your total domestic shipping cost was $2,295.00.
I also shipped some international packages. There were 40 of them, and each one cost 18.25 dollars to ship. What is the total international shipping cost?
That is 40 × 18.25. Since 18.25 × 4 = 73.00, multiplying by 10 gives 730. Your total international shipping cost was $730.00.
Please combine those two. What is my overall shipping total for the month?
Add the domestic and international totals: 2,295 + 730 = 3,025. Your overall shipping total for the month was $3,025.00.
Thanks. Here is a quick conversion question. How many kilometers are in 5 miles?
One mile is about 1.609 kilometers. So 5 miles is 5 × 1.609 = 8.045, which rounds to roughly 8.05 kilometers.
Okay. Back to the spreadsheet. I would like to add a row for the cost of goods. I made and sold 1,360 mugs at 14.00 dollars each in cost. What is the total cost of goods?
Multiply the units by the cost per unit: 1,360 × 14.00. That is 1,360 × 10 = 13,600 plus 1,360 × 4 = 5,440, which totals 19,040. Your total cost of goods was $19,040.00.
Now, using the revenue we found and that cost of goods number, what is the gross profit before shipping or taxes?

Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods. Using the monthly revenue of 33,320 and the cost of goods of 19,040, the calculation is 33,320 − 19,040 = 14,280. Your gross profit before shipping and taxes was $14,280.00. Note that this matches 1,360 mugs × 10.50 profit per mug, which is also 14,280, so the two methods agree.
Good check. A different question: how many ounces are in a pound?
There are 16 ounces in one pound in the standard avoirdupois system used in the United States for everyday weights.
Thanks. Now let us deal with sales tax. My local sales tax rate is 8.25 percent. If I apply that rate to my monthly revenue, what is the tax amount?

Convert 8.25 percent to a decimal, which is 0.0825, and multiply by the monthly revenue of 33,320. Breaking it up: 33,320 × 0.08 = 2,665.60, and 33,320 × 0.0025 = 83.30. Added together, that is 2,748.90. The sales tax amount is $2,748.90.
Is that tax something I collect from customers, or something I pay out of my own pocket?

In most places, sales tax is collected from customers at checkout and then passed on to the tax authority. So it is generally not part of your own profit. It is wise to keep it in a separate line in your spreadsheet so that it does not get mixed with your real revenue. Your local rules can vary, so it is worth confirming with your state or local tax office.
That makes sense. What is the capital of Canada?
The capital of Canada is Ottawa, which is in the province of Ontario, near the border with Quebec.
Good. Let me ask about packaging. I pay 0.85 dollars for each box, and I used one box per mug for 1,360 mugs. What is the total packaging cost?
Multiply the boxes by the price per box: 1,360 × 0.85. Since 1,360 × 0.80 = 1,088 and 1,360 × 0.05 = 68, the total is 1,156. Your total packaging cost was $1,156.00.
Now a quick temperature conversion. What is 72 degrees Fahrenheit in Celsius?
Subtract 32 and multiply by 5/9. So 72 − 32 = 40, and 40 × 5/9 = 22.2 when rounded to one decimal. Seventy-two degrees Fahrenheit is about 22.2 degrees Celsius.

Thank you. Next, my average order is bigger than I thought. Of the 340 domestic orders, how many mugs per order is that on average, if I sold 1,360 mugs in total? Assume all mugs were in domestic orders for this question.
Divide the mugs by the orders: 1,360 ÷ 340 = 4. So on average each order contained 4 mugs under that assumption. That is a useful figure for deciding whether to offer a four-pack discount.
Interesting. What does the word "frugal" mean?

"Frugal" means careful and economical with money or resources, avoiding waste. A frugal person buys what they need, compares prices, and does not spend on unnecessary extras. It is usually considered a positive trait, unlike "stingy," which suggests unwillingness to spend even when it is reasonable.
Okay. If I wanted to offer a 10 percent discount on the 24.50 price for a four-pack, what would be the discounted price per mug?
Ten percent of 24.50 is 2.45. Subtracting that from 24.50 gives 22.05. The discounted price per mug would be $22.05, so the four-pack would cost 4 × 22.05 = $88.20.
And what would the markup percentage be at that discounted price, using the same 14.00 cost?

The profit per mug at the discounted price is 22.05 − 14.00 = 8.05. Then 8.05 ÷ 14.00 = 0.575, so the markup would be 57.5 percent. That is lower than the 75 percent markup at full price, which is the trade-off of the discount.
Understood. How many centimeters are in an inch?
Good to know. I want to keep the spreadsheet tidy. Could you suggest how to label the rows we have computed so far?

Certainly. Here is a simple layout with one label per row: Unit price, Units sold, Monthly revenue, Unit cost, Markup percentage, Cost of goods, Gross profit, Domestic shipping, International shipping, Shipping total, Sales tax rate, Sales tax amount, and Packaging cost. Put the labels in column A and the values in column B, and use formulas for anything calculated so the cells update when an input changes.
That is clear. Which of those values are inputs and which are calculated?

The inputs are the ones you typed in: unit price, units sold, unit cost, domestic order count and average shipping cost, international package count and cost, tax rate, and packaging price per box. The calculated cells are monthly revenue, markup percentage, cost of goods, gross profit, the two shipping totals, the shipping total, the sales tax amount, and the packaging cost. Keeping the two groups visually separate, perhaps with different cell colors, helps avoid overwriting a formula by accident.
I will do that. What is the capital of Japan?
The capital of Japan is Tokyo.
Thank you. For one more idea, if my sales grow by 5 percent next month, how many mugs would I sell, starting from 1,360?
Five percent of 1,360 is 68. Adding it to 1,360 gives 1,428. You would sell 1,428 mugs next month with 5 percent growth.
And what revenue would that be at the regular price of 24.50?

Multiply 1,428 by 24.50. Calculating, 1,428 × 24 = 34,272 and 1,428 × 0.50 = 714, so the total is 34,986. Next month's projected revenue would be $34,986.00. That is 1,666 dollars more than the current monthly revenue of 33,320.
One more cost item. I pay a payment processor 2.9 percent of each sale plus 0.30 dollars per transaction. How much would that be on a single 24.50 dollar sale?

First the percentage part: 24.50 × 0.029 = 0.7105. Then add the flat fee of 0.30, which gives 1.0105. Rounded to the nearest cent, the fee on a single 24.50 dollar sale is about $1.01. Keep in mind that the processor charges per transaction, not per mug, so an order of four mugs would carry only one flat 0.30 fee.
Understood. What does the word "inventory" mean?

"Inventory" is the complete list of goods a business holds for sale, along with the materials used to make them. For your shop, it includes finished mugs on the shelf, unfired clay, glazes, and unused shipping boxes. Tracking inventory in a spreadsheet helps you avoid running out of stock or over-ordering supplies.
Okay. Suppose I have 2,000 mugs worth of clay and I use enough for 1,360 mugs. How many mugs worth of clay remain, and what percentage of the clay did I use?

The remainder is 2,000 − 1,360 = 640 mugs worth of clay. The share used is 1,360 ÷ 2,000 = 0.68, which is 68 percent. So you have 640 mugs worth of clay left, which is 32 percent of the original amount.
How many days are in a leap year?
A leap year has 366 days, because February has 29 days instead of the usual 28. Leap years occur roughly every four years, with some exceptions for century years that are not divisible by 400.
If I sell 1,360 mugs in a 30-day month, about how many mugs is that per day?

Divide 1,360 by 30. That equals 45.33 when rounded to two decimals. So you sell roughly 45 mugs per day on average. For planning, you might round up to 46 so that your daily stock estimate is a little generous.
What is the capital of Brazil?
The capital of Brazil is Brasilia. Like Canberra, it was built specifically to serve as the capital, and it replaced Rio de Janeiro in 1960.
Interesting. I also want to convert my shipping weight. A box with one mug weighs 1.5 pounds. How many ounces is that, using the 16 ounces per pound we discussed?
Multiply 1.5 by 16. That equals 24. A single boxed mug weighs 24 ounces. Four mugs in one box, ignoring any extra packing material, would weigh about 96 ounces, which is 6 pounds.
Good. How many kilograms is 6 pounds, roughly?
One pound is about 0.4536 kilograms. Multiplying, 6 × 0.4536 = 2.7216, so 6 pounds is roughly 2.72 kilograms.
I would like to price a larger set. If I sell a set of six mugs for 135.00 dollars, what is the price per mug, and is it higher or lower than the regular 24.50?

Divide 135.00 by 6, which equals 22.50 per mug. That is lower than the regular 24.50 by 2.00 dollars, so the set gives customers a discount of about 8.2 percent per mug (2.00 ÷ 24.50 = 0.0816). It is also slightly higher than the four-pack price of 22.05 per mug we calculated earlier, so the six-pack is a smaller discount than the four-pack.

"Scalable" describes something that can grow to handle more work without breaking down or becoming too costly. A scalable shop could go from selling 1,360 mugs a month to several thousand with the same basic process, perhaps by adding a second kiln or hiring a part-time packer. A spreadsheet with clear formulas is scalable in the same sense, because you only change the inputs.
Last question on units. How many square feet are in a room that is 12 feet by 15 feet? I want to know if my studio can fit another kiln.

Multiply the length by the width: 12 × 15 = 180. The room is 180 square feet. A typical small electric kiln needs a clearance zone of a few feet on every side, so a room of that size should be able to fit one more kiln, though you should check the manufacturer's clearance and ventilation requirements before buying.
Great. Thanks for all the help so far. I think I have a clear picture of the numbers now.

You are welcome. Let me know if you would like to combine any of them.

tests.title: Orders endpoint
tests.trap: A FastAPI stack and team rules stated early. A table described midway.
tests.question: Can you write the endpoint for paginated search over the orders table that we discussed?
turns: I would like to get some help with a few work items today. First, some background on my project so you have context. I work on a backend service written in Python 3.11 using FastAPI. The database is PostgreSQL 15, and we use SQLAlchemy 2.0 in async mode with the asyncpg driver. The service is deployed on Kubernetes. Two rules matter for everything we write. All endpoints must return a standard error envelope shaped like {"error": {"code": "...", "message": "..."}}, and we cannot add any new third-party dependencies without approval from the architecture group.

Thank you, that is a clear picture. To summarize: Python 3.11, FastAPI, PostgreSQL 15, SQLAlchemy 2.0 async with asyncpg, deployed on Kubernetes. Every endpoint returns errors in the envelope {"error": {"code", "message"}}, and any suggestion I make has to rely only on libraries you already have, which means FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, asyncpg, and the standard library. What would you like to start with?

Let us begin with a code review comment. A teammate opened a pull request that adds a helper function. The function takes a list of customer identifiers and calls the database once per identifier inside a for loop. I want to leave a comment that is constructive and specific. Can you draft one?

Here is a draft you can adapt: "Thanks for adding this helper. One concern is that it issues one query per customer identifier, so a list of five hundred identifiers produces five hundred round trips to the database. Could we fetch them in a single query using a WHERE customer_id IN (...) clause, or with the SQLAlchemy in_() operator, and then group the results in Python? That would keep latency predictable as the list grows. Happy to pair on it if useful." The comment names the problem, explains the impact, and offers a concrete alternative without sounding accusatory.
That works well. The teammate replied asking whether there is a limit on how many identifiers can go into an IN clause. What should I tell them?

PostgreSQL itself does not impose a small fixed limit on the number of items in an IN list, but there are practical constraints. The wire protocol allows at most 32,767 bind parameters per statement, and asyncpg enforces that. Very large lists can also produce slow query plans. A sensible guideline is to chunk the identifiers into batches of around one thousand and run one query per batch. For larger sets, passing an array parameter and using = ANY(:ids) keeps the statement text constant, which is friendlier to the plan cache.
Good. Now a small question about the service. In our FastAPI app, where should the code that translates exceptions into the error envelope live?

The cleanest place is a set of exception handlers registered on the application object. You define a small custom exception class, for example AppError, carrying a status code, an error code string, and a message. Then you register a handler with app.add_exception_handler that returns a JSONResponse whose body is {"error": {"code": exc.code, "message": exc.message}}. You should also override the handlers for RequestValidationError and for Starlette's HTTPException so that framework generated errors use the same envelope. Put all of this in a single module such as app/errors.py and call a register function from your application factory.
That matches what we have. Next, I need an outline for a design document. We are planning to add a background job that archives old records to cold storage. Can you propose a section outline?

Here is an outline you can use. 1. Summary: one paragraph describing the problem and the proposed solution. 2. Background and motivation: current table sizes, storage cost, and query performance issues. 3. Goals and non-goals: for example, archive records older than a retention threshold, and explicitly not changing the public API. 4. Proposed design: the job schedule, the selection criteria, the copy and delete sequence, and idempotency guarantees. 5. Data model changes: any new tables or columns. 6. Failure modes and recovery: partial failures, retries, and how to resume. 7. Observability: metrics, logs, and alerts. 8. Security and compliance considerations. 9. Rollout plan: feature flag, staging validation, and production phases. 10. Alternatives considered. 11. Open questions.
I like that. Under the proposed design section, what details do reviewers usually want to see for a job that deletes data?

Reviewers of destructive jobs generally look for several things. First, the exact selection predicate and how it is bounded, so the job cannot match more rows than intended. Second, the order of operations: copy to cold storage, verify the copy with a row count or checksum, and only then delete from the primary table. Third, batching, so that no single transaction holds locks for too long. Fourth, idempotency, meaning that rerunning the job after a crash does not duplicate or lose data. Fifth, a dry run mode that reports what would be archived. Finally, a clear rollback story, such as retaining archived data for a fixed period before it is purged for good.
Helpful. Let me switch to Git. I committed a change to the wrong branch. I have not pushed anything yet. How do I move that commit onto the correct branch?

Since nothing has been pushed, this is straightforward. First, note the commit hash with git log -1 on the wrong branch. Then switch to the correct branch with git checkout correct-branch and run git cherry-pick <hash> to apply the commit there. Return to the wrong branch and remove the commit with git reset --hard HEAD~1. If you had uncommitted work on that branch, stash it first with git stash so the reset does not discard it. Afterward, run git log on both branches to confirm each looks as expected.
Done, that worked. Is there a safer alternative to reset --hard?

Yes. You can use git reset --keep HEAD~1, which moves the branch back one commit but refuses to proceed if doing so would overwrite local changes. Another option is git branch backup-wrong-branch before resetting, which gives you a named pointer you can return to. You can also rely on git reflog, which records recent positions of HEAD for a while, so even after a hard reset you can usually recover the commit with git reflog followed by git checkout of the earlier entry.

Now I want to describe our data model, because I will be asking for help with an endpoint later. We have an orders table in PostgreSQL. Its columns are: id, a UUID primary key; customer_id, a UUID that references the customers table; status, a text column whose values are pending, paid, shipped, or cancelled; total_cents, a non-null integer; currency, a three character code such as USD; shipping_country, a two character country code; created_at, a timestamptz with a default of now(); and updated_at, also a timestamptz. There are indexes on customer_id, on status, and on created_at.

Thank you. To restate the orders table: id (UUID, primary key), customer_id (UUID, foreign key to customers), status (text: pending, paid, shipped, cancelled), total_cents (integer, not null), currency (three character code), shipping_country (two character code), created_at (timestamptz, default now()), and updated_at (timestamptz). Indexes exist on customer_id, status, and created_at. That is a good set of indexes for filtering and for ordering by creation time. Would you like me to write the SQLAlchemy model for it?
Not yet. I will come back to it. A different question: how should I name unit tests so that failures are easy to understand?

A common approach is to describe the behavior and the condition in the test name, for example test_create_order_returns_422_when_total_is_negative. The pattern test_<unit>_<expected result>_<condition> reads well in pytest output. Keep each test focused on one behavior so that a failure points to one cause. Group related tests in a class or a module named after the unit under test. Avoid vague names such as test_order_1 because they tell the reader nothing when the test fails in a continuous integration log.
I have a specific test that fails intermittently. It checks that an order's updated_at is later than its created_at after an update. Sometimes the two timestamps are equal. Why would that happen?

This usually happens because of timestamp resolution and transaction semantics. In PostgreSQL, now() returns the start time of the current transaction, not the wall clock time at the moment of the statement. If the order is created and updated within the same transaction, which is common in a test that uses a single session, both values are identical. Even across transactions, a very fast test may have two commits close enough that timestamps match at the precision you compare. The fix is to assert updated_at is greater than or equal to created_at, or to set the timestamps explicitly in the test, or to use clock_timestamp() in the update.

We do use a single session per test with a rollback at the end, so that explains it. I will assert greater than or equal and also check that updated_at changed from its previous value by setting it explicitly. Moving on: how do I run a FastAPI app with several worker processes on Kubernetes? I am wondering whether to use gunicorn.

Remember the dependency constraint: gunicorn would be a new third party package unless you already have it. If you do not, the simplest approach is to run uvicorn directly, which is presumably already a dependency, and scale horizontally by increasing the number of pod replicas rather than the number of processes per pod. On Kubernetes this is usually the preferred model anyway, because the platform handles restarts, health checks, and resource limits per pod. If you need multiple processes per container, uvicorn supports a --workers flag, though then CPU requests and limits should be sized accordingly.
We already use uvicorn, so I will keep one process per pod and rely on replicas. What should the readiness probe check?

A readiness probe should answer the question "can this pod serve traffic right now?" Typically that means an endpoint such as /health/ready that confirms the application has started and can acquire a connection from the database pool, for example by running SELECT 1 with a short timeout. Keep it fast and lightweight. The liveness probe should be simpler, checking only that the process is responsive, and it should not depend on the database. Otherwise a brief database outage could cause Kubernetes to restart every pod, which makes the incident worse. Both endpoints can return plain JSON on success, and on failure they should still use your error envelope.

That is a good distinction. Now let me ask for a review of a function signature. We have an async function get_order(session, order_id) that returns an order or None. A colleague wants it to raise an exception instead of returning None. Which is better?

Both are defensible, and the right answer depends on how the function is used. Returning None keeps the data access layer simple and lets callers decide what a missing row means. Raising an exception makes missing data impossible to ignore. A common compromise is to keep the repository function returning an Optional and to add a thin service layer function, such as get_order_or_404, that raises your AppError with a code like order_not_found and an HTTP status of 404. That way the endpoint produces the standard error envelope, and the lower layer remains reusable in contexts where a missing order is not an error.
I like that compromise. I will propose it. Next, a question about SQLAlchemy 2.0: what is the right way to create an async session dependency in FastAPI?

Create the engine once at startup with create_async_engine, using a postgresql+asyncpg URL. Build a session factory with async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False). Then define a dependency as an async generator: async def get_session() -> AsyncIterator[AsyncSession]: async with session_factory() as session: yield session. Endpoints receive it with session: AsyncSession = Depends(get_session). Setting expire_on_commit to False avoids lazy loading errors after commit, which cannot happen implicitly in async code. Dispose of the engine in the application's lifespan handler on shutdown.
Good. I am also being asked to write a short note for my manager about the risk of upgrading PostgreSQL from 15 to 16. Can you help me outline it?

Certainly. A short risk note could have these parts. First, a one paragraph summary of the proposal and the recommendation. Second, benefits: performance improvements in query planning and parallelism, plus continued support timelines. Third, risks: extension compatibility, changes in query plans that may affect slow queries, and the downtime or replication complexity of a major version upgrade. Fourth, mitigation: testing on a staging copy of production data, comparing query plans for the critical queries, and having a tested rollback plan. Fifth, a proposed timeline and the people required. Finish with a clear ask, such as approval to begin staging validation.
That is concise enough. What is a good way to compare query plans before and after an upgrade?

Collect a representative set of your most important queries, using pg_stat_statements if it is enabled, which shows the heaviest queries by total time. On the current version, run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for each and save the output. After restoring a production snapshot to a version 16 staging instance, run ANALYZE so statistics are fresh, then repeat the EXPLAIN commands. Compare the plan shapes, estimated versus actual rows, and execution time. Flag any query whose plan type changed, such as an index scan becoming a sequential scan, or whose time regressed by more than a threshold you agree on in advance.
Understood. Back to the service. I want to define a Pydantic model for query parameters. Is it acceptable to use Pydantic v2 features like model_validator?

If your project is already on Pydantic v2, which is the version FastAPI has supported for some time, then model_validator and field_validator are part of the library you already depend on, so there is no new dependency. Check your lock file to confirm the major version. Pydantic v2 uses field_validator with a classmethod decorator instead of the older validator decorator. For query parameters, you can declare a model and receive it with Annotated[FilterParams, Query()], which FastAPI supports in recent releases.

We are on Pydantic v2 and a recent FastAPI. Here is the next decision. For the orders search endpoint I want to support filtering by status, by customer_id, and by a created_at date range, with pagination using page and page_size parameters. Page size defaults to 25 with a maximum of 100. Results should be sorted by created_at descending, and the response should include the total count. Does that seem reasonable?

That design is reasonable and fits the indexes you have. Filtering on status, customer_id, and created_at each has an index, and ordering by created_at descending can use the created_at index. A few notes. Offset pagination is simple and acceptable at moderate table sizes, though deep pages get slower, and the total count query can be costly on a very large table. Add a secondary sort on id so ordering is deterministic when two orders share a created_at value. Validate that page is at least 1 and page_size is between 1 and 100, and return validation failures in the error envelope.
Agreed on the secondary sort by id. I will ask you to write that endpoint later. For now, let me ask about logging. What fields should we include in structured logs for each request?

A useful baseline is a timestamp, log level, service name, a request or correlation identifier, the HTTP method, the path template rather than the raw path, the status code, and the duration in milliseconds. Include the authenticated principal or tenant identifier if you have one, but avoid logging request bodies or anything personal. Generate a request identifier in middleware, accept one from an upstream header if present, and return it in a response header so support can match user reports to logs. The standard library logging module with a JSON formatter you write yourself avoids a new dependency.
Good point on the dependency. I have a question about Git again. What is the difference between merge and rebase when updating a feature branch?

Merging main into your feature branch creates a merge commit that joins the two histories. It preserves exactly what happened and never rewrites commits, but it can clutter history with merge commits. Rebasing replays your feature commits on top of the latest main, producing a linear history, but it rewrites your commits, so their hashes change. The practical rule is to rebase only branches that nobody else is building on, and never rebase commits that have been shared. If your team squashes on merge, either approach produces a clean main, so choose whichever your team prefers.

We squash on merge, so I will merge main into my branch. Now another code review item. A teammate wrote an endpoint that catches a bare except and returns a 500 with the exception message in the response. How should I comment on that?

Here is a possible comment: "Two concerns here. Catching a bare except will also swallow exceptions like KeyboardInterrupt and cancellation errors, which can make shutdown and timeouts behave unexpectedly. Please catch the specific exceptions you expect. Also, returning the raw exception message to the client can leak internal details such as table names or connection strings. Could we log the full exception with the request identifier and return a generic message in the standard error envelope, for example code internal_error and message 'An unexpected error occurred'?" That keeps the feedback tied to your team convention.
Thanks. For the design document, I also need to describe observability for the archive job. What metrics should I include?

For a batch job, I would propose these metrics. Counters for rows selected, rows copied, rows deleted, and rows that failed. A gauge or histogram for batch duration. A gauge for the age of the oldest record eligible for archiving, which shows whether the job is keeping up. A counter for job runs labeled by outcome, success or failure. A timestamp gauge for the last successful run so you can alert if the job has not succeeded within an expected window. Add log lines at the start and end of each run with the totals, and alert on failure counts and on a stale last success time.
Good. I have another question about testing async code. How do I write an async test with pytest if we cannot add dependencies?

That depends on what is already installed. If pytest-asyncio or anyio is already in your dev dependencies, you can mark tests with the corresponding marker. Note that anyio is installed as a dependency of Starlette, so its pytest plugin is available in most FastAPI projects: mark a test with pytest.mark.anyio and provide an anyio_backend fixture returning asyncio. For HTTP calls, httpx with ASGITransport can drive the app directly, assuming httpx is already present, which it commonly is as the basis for the Starlette test client. Confirm against your lock file before relying on any of these.
We do have pytest-asyncio. What is the right way to isolate database state between tests?

The most common pattern is to open a connection, begin an outer transaction, bind a session to that connection, and roll the transaction back at the end of each test. In SQLAlchemy 2.0 you can create the session with join_transaction_mode set to "create_savepoint", so that commits inside the code under test become savepoints and the outer rollback still discards everything. Your session fixture yields the session, and your dependency override for get_session returns it. This is fast, because no data is truncated, and it keeps tests independent of one another.
That is what we use. Next I want advice on writing a short incident summary. We had a brief outage yesterday because a database migration locked a table. Can you suggest a structure?

A blameless incident summary usually contains these parts. Impact: who was affected, for how long, and how severely. Timeline: key timestamps from detection to resolution. Root cause: a migration added a column with a default on a large table and held an exclusive lock longer than expected. Detection: how the team noticed. Resolution: what stopped the impact. Contributing factors: for example, no lock timeout configured and no staging test at production scale. Action items: each with an owner and a due date, such as setting lock_timeout in migrations and adding a review checklist item for table-locking operations.
Useful. Related to that, how can we run migrations more safely in PostgreSQL 15?

Several practices help. Set lock_timeout and statement_timeout at the start of each migration so a migration fails fast instead of queueing behind long transactions and blocking everything else. Create indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which in Alembic requires running outside a transaction. Adding a nullable column without a default is instant, and since PostgreSQL 11, adding a column with a constant default is also a metadata-only change. Add constraints in two steps, first as NOT VALID and then validating separately. Finally, run migrations as a separate Kubernetes job before the rollout rather than at pod startup.
Good guidance. Let me ask something small about the service: what HTTP status should we return when a client sends a status filter value that is not one of the four allowed values?

A 422 Unprocessable Entity is the convention in FastAPI for request validation failures, and it is what you get automatically if you declare the parameter as a Literal or an Enum. Since your team requires the error envelope, your RequestValidationError handler should convert the default detail list into something like {"error": {"code": "validation_error", "message": "status must be one of pending, paid, shipped, cancelled"}}. Some teams use 400 instead, so if you have an existing convention, follow it. Consistency across endpoints is more important than the particular choice.
We use 422 with the code validation_error. Now, another design document question. How do I write the alternatives considered section well?

Present each alternative fairly, as if its advocate were reading it. For each one, give a short description, the main advantages, the main disadvantages, and the reason it was not chosen. Tie the reasons to the goals you listed earlier, so the reader can see the decision follows from the stated priorities. For the archive job, alternatives might include PostgreSQL table partitioning with detaching old partitions, a managed cold storage export tool, or doing nothing and upgrading storage. Always include "do nothing" with its real cost, because it frames the value of the work.
I will include partitioning. In fact, would partitioning the orders table by created_at be a good idea?

It could be, depending on the size and access pattern. Range partitioning by created_at is a natural fit when most queries target recent data and old data is archived or dropped in bulk, since detaching or dropping a partition is nearly instant compared with deleting millions of rows. The trade-offs are that the primary key must include the partition key, so a primary key on id alone is not possible on a partitioned table, and foreign keys referencing it become more complicated. For a table with a UUID primary key that is referenced elsewhere, that is a significant change that deserves its own design review.
That is a real constraint, so I will note it as a risk. A smaller question: should timestamps in API responses be in UTC?

Yes. Store timestamps as timestamptz, which PostgreSQL normalizes to UTC internally, and serialize them in ISO 8601 format with a UTC offset, for example 2026-11-06T14:30:00Z. Pydantic v2 serializes timezone-aware datetime objects in that form. Make sure the datetime values you create in Python are timezone-aware, using datetime.now(timezone.utc) rather than datetime.utcnow(), which returns a naive value and is deprecated in Python 3.12. Clients can then convert to a local time zone for display.
Good. I want to review a pull request description template. What should be in a good one?

A good pull request description answers four questions. What changed, in a sentence or two. Why it changed, with a link to the ticket or design document. How it was tested, including any manual steps. What reviewers should look at closely, such as a risky migration or a change in public behavior. Optional sections include screenshots, rollout notes, and a checklist covering tests added, documentation updated, and feature flags in place. Keep the template short. A long template tends to be filled out carelessly, while a short one is read and used.
I will suggest that to the team. Another Git question: how do I undo a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch?

Use git revert <hash>, which creates a new commit that reverses the changes and leaves history intact. This is the safe choice on a shared branch because nobody has to rewrite their local history. For a merge commit, use git revert -m 1 <hash> to specify the mainline parent. Avoid git reset followed by a force push on a shared branch, since it rewrites history others may already have pulled. If the original change is later fixed, remember that reverting a merge means you may need to revert the revert before merging the corrected branch again.
Clear. Now a unit test question. I have a test that mocks the database session with a MagicMock, but awaiting the mock raises a TypeError. What is wrong?

A regular MagicMock is not awaitable, so awaiting its return value raises a TypeError. Since Python 3.8, the standard library provides AsyncMock in unittest.mock. Use AsyncMock for the session methods that are awaited, such as execute and commit, for example session = AsyncMock(spec=AsyncSession). Note that session.add is synchronous in SQLAlchemy, so for that method use a regular MagicMock; with spec set on an AsyncMock, the library chooses the correct kind automatically for each attribute. That said, for database code, tests against a real PostgreSQL instance with rollback usually give more reliable results than mocks.
That fixed it, thank you. I am considering adding a rate limiting library, but I know about the dependency rule. What would you suggest?

Without approval, the options are to implement a simple limiter yourself or to push the concern to infrastructure. A minimal in-process token bucket in a middleware is easy to write, but it only limits per pod, which is imprecise when you run several replicas. A better approach on Kubernetes is to enforce rate limits at the ingress or API gateway layer, for example with the ingress controller's built-in annotations, which requires no application dependency. If you need per-user limits that must be accurate across pods, that is a reasonable justification to request approval for a library backed by Redis.
Rate limiting at the ingress is a good idea. I will raise it with the platform team. Let me ask one more design question for the document: should the archive job run as a Kubernetes CronJob?

Yes, a CronJob is a natural fit for a scheduled, finite task. Set concurrencyPolicy to Forbid so two runs never overlap, give it a reasonable activeDeadlineSeconds, and set backoffLimit to control retries. Because the job deletes data, make the work idempotent and resumable by processing in bounded batches and recording progress. Configure resource requests and limits, and use a dedicated database role with only the permissions it needs. Emit the metrics we discussed, and set startingDeadlineSeconds so that a missed schedule does not trigger a surprising burst of catch-up runs.

Good. I think I have what I need for the design document. Now, going back to the service. We have discussed the orders table, the filters, the pagination rules, and the error envelope. Let me also confirm one thing: the response for a list should be an object with items, page, page_size, and total, correct?

Yes, that is a common and clean shape. An object with items (the list of orders), page, page_size, and total lets clients render pagination controls without guessing. If you later switch to cursor-based pagination, you can version the endpoint or add a next_cursor field. Keep the order representation consistent with the single order endpoint, so clients use one schema for both, and make sure total counts only rows matching the active filters.
Yes, that is the shape I want. One last general question before I move on: how can I keep my pull requests small?

Aim for one logical change per pull request. Separate refactoring from behavior changes, so reviewers can check each on its own. Land schema migrations in their own pull request ahead of the code that uses them. Use feature flags to merge incomplete work safely. Stack changes in sequence when a feature is large, and describe the order in each description. As a rough guide, changes under about four hundred lines receive noticeably better reviews than larger ones, because reviewers can hold the whole change in their heads.

```python
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Literal
from uuid import UUID

from pydantic import AwareDatetime, BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, model_validator

OrderStatus = Literal["pending", "paid", "shipped", "cancelled"]


class OrderSearchParams(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")  # unknown query params -> 422

    status: OrderStatus | None = None
    customer_id: UUID | None = None
    created_from: AwareDatetime | None = None  # inclusive
    created_to: AwareDatetime | None = None    # exclusive
    page: int = Field(1, ge=1)
    page_size: int = Field(25, ge=1, le=100)

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_date_range(self) -> "OrderSearchParams":
        if (
            self.created_from is not None
            and self.created_to is not None
            and self.created_from >= self.created_to
        ):
            raise ValueError("created_from must be earlier than created_to")
        return self


class OrderOut(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)

    id: UUID
    customer_id: UUID
    status: OrderStatus
    total_cents: int
    currency: str
    shipping_country: str
    created_at: datetime
    updated_at: datetime | None


class OrderPage(BaseModel):
    items: list[OrderOut]
    page: int
    page_size: int
    total: int
```

**app/orders/repository.py**
```python
from sqlalchemy import func, select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.orders.models import Order
from app.orders.schemas import OrderSearchParams


async def search_orders(
    session: AsyncSession, params: OrderSearchParams
) -> tuple[list[Order], int]:
    filters = []
    if params.status is not None:
        filters.append(Order.status == params.status)
    if params.customer_id is not None:
        filters.append(Order.customer_id == params.customer_id)
    if params.created_from is not None:
        filters.append(Order.created_at >= params.created_from)
    if params.created_to is not None:
        filters.append(Order.created_at < params.created_to)

    total = await session.scalar(
        select(func.count()).select_from(Order).where(*filters)
    )

    result = await session.scalars(
        select(Order)
        .where(*filters)
        .order_by(Order.created_at.desc(), Order.id.desc())
        .limit(params.page_size)
        .offset((params.page - 1) * params.page_size)
    )
    return list(result), total or 0
```

**app/orders/router.py**
```python
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, Query
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.db import get_session
from app.orders.repository import search_orders
from app.orders.schemas import OrderOut, OrderPage, OrderSearchParams

router = APIRouter(prefix="/orders", tags=["orders"])


@router.get("", response_model=OrderPage)
async def list_orders(
    params: Annotated[OrderSearchParams, Query()],
    session: Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(get_session)],
) -> OrderPage:
    orders, total = await search_orders(session, params)
    return OrderPage(
        items=[OrderOut.model_validate(o) for o in orders],
        page=params.page,
        page_size=params.page_size,
        total=total,
    )
```

A few decisions to check:

- **Date range is half-open,** `[created_from, created_to)`, so consecutive ranges such as one month followed by the next never double-count an order. `AwareDatetime` rejects timestamps without a timezone, which avoids clients silently querying in the wrong zone.
- **Unknown query parameters are rejected** because of `extra="forbid"`. A typo like `?stauts=paid` then fails loudly instead of quietly returning unfiltered results. Remove that line if you'd rather ignore extra parameters.
- **Requesting a page past the end** returns an empty `items` list with the correct `total`, not a 404. That is the usual behavior, and clients can work out the last page from `total`.
- **The model_validator message gets a prefix:** Pydantic delivers it as "Value error, created_from must be earlier than created_to". If your handler passes `msg` through unchanged, you may want to strip that prefix there.
- **The two queries run one after the other** on purpose. A single AsyncSession can't run statements concurrently, so don't wrap them in `asyncio.gather`.
- **Indexing:** the single-column indexes work, but the common query "one customer's orders, newest first" would benefit from a composite index on `(customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`. If you add it, use a separate migration with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.

Then register it with `app.include_router(router)` in your application factory. I can write the tests next, using your rollback-per-test session fixture and httpx with ASGITransport.

ORDER_STATUSES = ("pending", "paid", "shipped", "cancelled")


def _as_utc(value: datetime) -> datetime:
    # Naive input is treated as UTC; aware input is converted to UTC.
    if value.tzinfo is None:
        return value.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    return value.astimezone(timezone.utc)

    def check_status(cls, v: str | None) -> str | None:
        if v is not None and v not in ORDER_STATUSES:
            raise ValueError(f"status must be one of {', '.join(ORDER_STATUSES)}")
        return v

    @field_validator("created_from")
    @classmethod
    def normalize_from(cls, v: datetime | None) -> datetime | None:
        return _as_utc(v) if v is not None else None

    @field_validator("created_to")
    @classmethod
    def normalize_to(cls, v: datetime | None, info: ValidationInfo) -> datetime | None:
        if v is None:

        v = _as_utc(v)
